Overview and scope
The question asks which determinants of English proficiency continue to show statistical significance once socioeconomic status (SES), prior education, and cognitive ability are held constant. Across bilingual child, secondary/tertiary student, and EMI/ELL contexts, multivariate and longitudinal models converge on a set of factors—school context and program type, cognitive-affective processes (e.g., executive function, motivation), language-specific inputs (heritage language proficiency, English exposure quality/quantity), and structural school factors (streaming/track and rural–urban context)—as persistent predictors even after accounting for SES, prior education, and general cognitive ability. Some studies also show SES diminishing or becoming non-significant when mediated by proficiency or when richer school- and cognition-related controls are included. 

What remains significant after controlling for SES, prior education, and cognitive ability

1) School context and program structure
- School type and tracking are robust: students in university-track/academic tracks score significantly higher on English proficiency tests than those in vocational tracks, even after controlling for parental education and cognitive ability, indicating structural school context matters beyond family background and raw cognition <cite id="488bbf33-3">variables pertaining to cognition clearly show a strong effect on the C-test results in English, and the type of school also affects the C-test results crucially; students who attend university-bound secondary schools score significantly better in English than those in vocational-track schools</cite>. 
- In multilingual/heritage samples modeled with multiple linear regression (with two-way interactions), school year and school type remain in final models alongside cognitive ability, gender, and language proficiency predictors, underscoring the continuing role of school context and grade progression in proficiency trajectories <cite id="127a20b5-4">multiple linear regressions tracked the strength and contribution of each variable to English proficiency models including cognitive ability, socioeconomic status, German proficiency (heritage), heritage language proficiency, school type (Gymnasium vs other), school year, and gender</cite>. 
- In EMI/secondary settings, ELL status and achievement remain significant predictors of outcomes downstream (e.g., postsecondary enrollment) even after adding SES and language proficiency controls, showing that structural academic positioning (e.g., EMI curriculum, achievement gaps) persists beyond background and basic proficiency <cite id="127a20b5-0">adding achievement variables improved model fit; 10th-grade ELA scores strongly predicted postsecondary enrollment; ELLs from lower-SES households had lower enrollment likelihood; in urban schools, holding all else equal, ELLs were 15 percentage points less likely to enroll in university than native English speakers</cite>. 
- Rural vs. urban school context independently affects outcomes for ELLs, persisting even when achievement and SES are included, suggesting school ecology and resource/access remain consequential once baseline academic performance and family background are controlled <cite id="127a20b5-0">ELLs from rural schools were associated with higher likelihood of attending any postsecondary institution than ELLs in more urban settings by about 13–15 percentage points; achievement and SES indicators remained significant and interacted with ELL status</cite>. 

2) Cognitive-affective mechanisms beyond general ability
- Executive functions, especially cognitive flexibility, predict English proficiency-related outcomes (GPA, Math, ELA) independently across regression models, indicating metacognitive/regulatory processes as significant contributors beyond general cognitive ability and prior schooling <cite id="127a20b5-3">cognitive flexibility consistently predicted GPA, Math, and ELA scores across multiple regression models; students described help-seeking, study routines, and planning behaviors reflecting executive functioning, which supported classroom engagement despite language barriers</cite>. 
- Behavioral and emotional problems (BEP) reported by parents and teachers negatively associate with GPA and Math even after accounting for SES and achievement, highlighting socio-emotional functioning as a significant factor that interacts with language access and academic performance <cite id="127a20b5-3">higher BEP was negatively associated with GPA and Math scores; students reported stress, anxiety, and social withdrawal in response to language barriers and academic demands</cite>. 
- Motivation and self-evaluation show positive associations with English test performance in whole-population analyses, although effects can attenuate when focusing only on bilingual subgroups, implying that motivational and self-regulatory factors are significant but may be partially confounded by subgroup-specific cognitive/linguistic profiles when SES and ability are controlled <cite id="488bbf33-3">motivation has a positive effect on English results in the entire population; higher self-assessment in English has a positive impact on C-test scores, but motivation is not significant once considering only bilinguals</cite>. 

3) Language-specific inputs and bilingual repertoires
- Cumulative English exposure (input quantity) interacts significantly with SES proxies (input quality), and composite SES measures (parental education and occupation) remain informative predictors of English proficiency even after accounting for exposure alone, indicating that family background shapes input quality/quantity in ways that persist once raw exposure is controlled <cite id="488bbf33-4">alternative SES measures interacted significantly with cumulative English exposure as predictors of English proficiency; the composite measure nesting parental occupation in parental education was the most informative predictor</cite>. 
- Heritage language proficiency (e.g., German/L1) and English receptive vocabulary are modeled as distinct, significant predictors of English proficiency, with ERP and regression evidence showing language proficiency components and their interactions with SES and age of acquisition remain after controls, pointing to bilingual repertoire dynamics as key mechanisms beyond general ability and SES <cite id="272b3b9e-2">children were divided into higher vs lower L2-proficiency groups by a median split on the CELF receptive language subtest, controlling for age, SES, and age of L2 acquisition; groups differed in receptive vocabulary</cite><cite id="127a20b5-4">heritage language proficiency (if applicable) was added as an additional predictor in separate analyses of English proficiency with cognitive ability, SES, German proficiency, school type, school year, and gender</cite>. 
- In EMI/foreign-language settings, parental education level (as a proxy for educational status) can capture part of SES influence; once parents’ education is included alongside SES indicators, SES may not add uniquely significant variance for proficiency, emphasizing family language capital as a durable predictor beyond income/occupation alone <cite id="488bbf33-3">SES did not contribute significantly to explaining performance in English once additional predictor variables were included; school-type and parental education (educational status) show strong effects; income and occupation may be less reliable than parents’ educational level in assessing SES</cite>. 

4) Gender and subgroup characteristics
- Gender remains associated with English proficiency in multivariate models, with evidence that group differences (e.g., monolingual vs bilingual) can modulate the role of SES and add unique variance in proficiency outcomes when included as predictors <cite id="488bbf33-3">intriguingly, socioeconomic status did not turn out to contribute significantly once school-type and cognitive variables were included; school-type and cognitive ability were strong predictors, and monolinguals outperformed bilinguals overall</cite>. 
- ELL status itself continues to be a robust negative predictor of academic performance on standardized tests and postsecondary transitions even after adding SES and achievement variables, indicating persistent language access barriers beyond family background and prior schooling <cite id="127a20b5-3">ELL status was a robust negative predictor of standardized Math and ELA outcomes but not GPA, aligning with research on how limited English proficiency undermines access to curriculum and assessment performance</cite><cite id="127a20b5-0">achievement strongly predicted postsecondary enrollment; ELLs from lower-SES households had lower enrollment likelihood; in urban schools, ELLs were 15 percentage points less likely to enroll in university than native speakers when holding all else equal</cite>. 

5) Domain-specific and item-response measurement factors
- In large-scale assessments, models that incorporate ELL status, grade level, and their interactions show measurement shifts across developmental stages, implying that developmental trajectory and language access conditions affect proficiency measurement beyond static SES and prior test scores, with differential item functioning by ELL group indicating structural test features also remain relevant controls <cite id="127a20b5-1">the full explanatory model included ELL status (dummies for ELL, exited-ELL, non-ELL), grade level, and their interaction to evaluate DIF and parameter drift across grades</cite><cite id="127a20b5-3">convergences between regression models and qualitative narratives confirmed ELL status strongly influences outcomes and that limited English proficiency undermines classroom participation, comprehension, and confidence</cite>. 

When do SES effects diminish or change?
- SES can lose independent significance when proficiency-related mediators are included; for example, in an EMI university sample, SES predicted English proficiency and achievement but stopped being significant once English proficiency was mediated, suggesting SES influences operate partly through proficiency pathways <cite id="488bbf3b3-1">SES significantly predicted students’ academic achievement and English proficiency; however, it stopped being a significant predictor when mediated through English proficiency</cite>. 
- Conversely, SES proxies tied to input quality retain strong interactions with exposure and predict proficiency even after controlling for prior education and ability, indicating that family-based input quality/quantity remains a distinct mechanism from raw prior schooling and general cognition <cite id="488bbf33-4">SES operationalizations interacted significantly with cumulative English exposure to predict proficiency; composite SES measures (parental education and occupation) were the most informative</cite>. 
- When school type and cognitive measures are added, SES may not uniquely add to variance, pointing to school context and cognition as stronger or more proximal determinants in some settings <cite id="488bbf33-3">SES did not contribute significantly to explaining performance in English once additional predictors (school-type, cognitive ability) were included</cite>. 

Which factors tend to attenuate or become non-significant
- Pure SES indicators can attenuate when cognitively demanding school context and English proficiency are controlled; parental education (as a proxy for educational capital) may capture part of SES influence, and in some models SES ceases to be a unique predictor once proficiency pathways and school type are modeled <cite id="488bbf33-3">SES did not turn out to contribute significantly once school-type and cognition were included; parental education (educational status) may be more objective than income/occupation</cite>. 
- Prior education loads heavily on achievement models, but achievement itself becomes a stronger, persistent predictor of downstream outcomes (e.g., postsecondary enrollment), with ELL status adding independent negative effects beyond achievement and SES in school contexts <cite id="127a20b5-0">achievement variables improved model fit; ELA scores strongly predicted postsecondary enrollment; ELLs from lower-SES households had lower likelihood of enrollment; ELLs in urban schools were 15 points less likely to enroll in university than natives when holding all else equal</cite>. 
- General cognitive ability is strongly associated with English proficiency and often remains significant, but specific cognitive-affective mechanisms (executive function, motivation) and school context frequently provide incremental explanatory power beyond general ability when included in the same models <cite id="488bbf33-3">variables pertaining to cognition show strong effects on C-test; school type affects English scores crucially</cite><cite id="127a20b5-3">cognitive flexibility predicted GPA, Math, and ELA; behavioral/emotional problems negatively associated with academic performance</cite>. 

Implications and remaining uncertainties
- Across contexts, three classes of factors tend to remain significant when SES, prior education, and broad cognitive ability are controlled: (a) school/program context (tracking, EMI/immersion vs. bilingual programs, rural–urban ecology), (b) specific cognitive-affective mechanisms (executive function, motivation/self-efficacy, socio-emotional problems), and (c) language-specific inputs (heritage language proficiency, English exposure quality/quantity, parental educational capital shaping input) <cite id="488bbf33-3">school-type and cognition strongly predict English performance; SES may not add once these are in the model</cite><cite id="127a20b5-3">ELL status, executive function, and behavioral/emotional problems independently predict outcomes</cite><cite id="488bbf33-4">composite SES (parental education/occupation) interacts with English exposure to predict proficiency</cite>. 
- The exact significance of “home literacy” and parental language exposure per se is context-dependent; some studies capture these via parental education (as a proxy for educational capital and input quality) and find persistent effects, but direct home literacy measures are less frequently modeled alongside SES, prior education, and ability in the retrieved evidence, indicating a gap and a need for targeted multivariate analyses on home literacy environments in ELL cohorts <cite id="488bbf33-3">SES may be partially contained in parents’ education; income/occupation may be less reliable than parents’ educational level</cite><cite id="272b3b9e-2">maternal education used as a control for SES when comparing higher vs lower L2-proficiency groups; groups differed on receptive vocabulary</cite>. 
- Finally, motivation and self-assessment effects can vary by subgroup (e.g., bilingual-only vs whole population), suggesting that within-group heterogeneity and measurement of proficiency may alter significance, reinforcing the importance of multigroup modeling and proficiency-specific indicators when interpreting effects after controls <cite id="488bbf33-3">motivation shows positive effects on English overall but not when considering only bilinguals; self-assessment in English positively affects C-test scores</cite>. 

Practical summary for policy and instruction
- Investing in academic stream alignment away from early vocational separation, and in EMI/English immersion quality when appropriate, should yield gains because school type and program structure remain significant after controls <cite id="488bbf33-3">university-bound tracks score significantly better in English than vocational-track schools</cite>. 
- Targeted development of executive function, socio-emotional regulation, and motivation (with family/teacher scaffolds) can improve English proficiency beyond general ability and SES, with measurable returns to GPA, ELA, and math <cite id="127a20b5-3">cognitive flexibility and executive functioning consistently predicted academic outcomes; scaffolding by family/teacher support related to reported metacognitive and planning behaviors</cite>. 
- Strengthening bilingual repertoires and English input quality/quantity—through parental education support, heritage language programming, and enriched English literacy—are likely to remain effective levers even after accounting for SES and prior schooling, as their unique contributions are observed in regression and interaction models <cite id="127a20b5-4">heritage language proficiency and school context significantly contributed to English proficiency models</cite><cite id="488bbf33-4">SES-proxies interacted with cumulative English exposure to predict proficiency; composite parental education/occupation provided the most information</cite>. 

In sum, when socioeconomic status, prior education, and cognitive ability are controlled, English proficiency differences are robustly explained by school/program context, cognitive-affective mechanisms, and language-specific inputs, with ELL status and rural/urban schooling continuing to mark persistent barriers and advantages respectively, even as SES effects often attenuate once richer cognitive and contextual controls are included <cite id="488bbf33-3">SES may not add once school-type and cognition are included; cognitive ability and school type strongly affect English performance</cite><cite id="127a20b5-3">ELL status robustly predicts standardized outcome gaps; executive function and behavioral/emotional problems independently predict performance</cite><cite id="488bbf33-4">composite SES interacts with English exposure to predict proficiency</cite><cite id="127a20b5-0">achievement and ELL status jointly predict postsecondary enrollment with persistent SES interactions</cite>.

Title: Socioeconomic status as a proxy for input quality in bilingual children?
Snippet: Abstract This study investigates the effect of socioeconomic status (SES) as a proxy for input quality, in predicting language proficiency. Different operationalizations of SES are compared, including simple measures (parental education and parental occupation) and complex measures combining two dimensions (among parental education, parental occupation, and deprivation risk). All significantly predict overall English proficiency scores in a diverse group of 5- to 7-year-olds acquiring English and another language. The most informative SES measure in that respect is shown to be a complex measure combining parental education and parental occupation. That measure is used in a second set of analyses showing that different aspects of language are affected differently by variations in SES and in language exposure.

Title: When Proficiency and Education Matter: The Mediating Role of English Proficiency and Moderating Effect of Parents’ Education in the SES–Academic Achievement Relationship During EMI
Snippet: This study investigated how socioeconomic status (SES) is associated with academic achievement and English proficiency in an English-medium instruction (EMI) program at a state university in Indonesia. It also examined the mediating effect of English proficiency and moderating effect of parents’ education on the relationship between SES and academic achievement. Data for 234 EMI students were obtained from the academic office of the university. Based on mediation analysis, SES significantly predicted students’ academic achievement and English proficiency. However, it stopped being a significant predictor when mediated through English proficiency. The moderation analysis shows that the degree of increase in EMI students’ grade point average was affected by the level of parents’ education when associated with family income. The article also presents the implications of the findings in enhancing university EMI programs and suggestions for future research.

Title: INVESTIGATING THE RELATION BETWEEN PROFICIENCY OF LANGUAGE AND COGNITIVE SKILLS AMONGST UNDERGRADUATE STUDENTS: A QUANTATITIVE CASE STUDY
Snippet: This quantitative correlational study investigates the relationship between English language proficiency and cognitive skills among 150 participants aged 18–35 from diverse linguistic backgrounds. Pearson correlation analysis revealed significant positive relationships between English proficiency and multiple dimensions of cognitive ability. Title: Socioeconomic status as a proxy for input quality in bilingual children?
Snippet: The first part of the paper investigated the interaction between cumulative English exposure (as a proxy for input quantity) and SES (as a proxy for input quality) as predictors of proficiency in the school language in a socioeconomically diverse group of 5-to 7-year-old bilinguals schooled in English.

Hypothesis 1 was that parental education would be an important dimension of SES as a predictor of the child's language proficiency (Hoff et al., 2017). Six alternative measures of SES were considered: two simple measures (parental occupation and parental education) and four complex measures (two combining parental occupation and education, and two combining parental occupation and deprivation risk). All the alternative measures were shown to interact significantly with cumulative English exposure as predictors of English proficiency (indexed by a global measure derived through PCA). Out of the six alternatives, the composite measure obtained by nesting parental occupation in parental education was shown to be the most informative, as a predictor of English proficiency. Hypothesis 1a was not confirmed: a simple SES measure based on parental education is not the most informative as a predictor of English proficiency. Hypothesis 1b was confirmed: among alternative composite SES measures, the one assigning a strong weight to parental education was more informative as predictor of proficiency than alternative SES measures. While parental education is significantly associated with parental occupation, the two dimensions also contribute independently to predicting proficiency scores in this population sample.

Importantly, the association between parental education and occupation was modulated by "bilingualism" in our population sample (in spite of the fact that children had been recruited from the same schools). This is in line with other studies, which have found that SES is associated with ethnicity (Fairley et al., 2014), and that the language input experienced by children varies within SES groups (Schwab & Lew-Williams, 2016). Composite measures of SES are therefore likely to be more informative (as also advocated by Gatt et al., 2020), to the extent that they are sensitive to variability in the association between dimensions of SES.

Snippet: As described earlier, we evaluated the role of two student characteristics, ELL status conceptualized as a potential source of DIF and grade level conceptualized as a potential source of parameter drift across developmental stages. This design employed student characteristics as features of the measurement model. 

This study was conducted based on data gathered in an urban district in the state of Texas. Latino students who participated in the assessment are included in this secondary data analysis, including students in 6th through 12th grade. In addition, students were classified as (a) receiving ELL services, (b) received but exited ELL services, or (c) never received and/or never were eligible for ELL services. To receive ELL services, students report a home language other than English, are evaluated to determine their level of English proficiency, and receive a Broad English Ability score of 4 or lower on the Woodcock-Muñoz Language Survey-Revised. Latino students who have exited ELL services have satisfied their ELL learning goals, performed at the advanced level (or lower with additional evidence of proficiency) on the Oregon English Language Proficiency Assessment, and have the ability to participate meaningfully in the general education program. Latino students who are not ELL students are those for whom English is their primary language.

Title: English Language Learners and Their Postsecondary Education Outcomes: Evidence From Arkansas
Snippet: From this robustness check, we found that adding these achievement variables indeed improved the model fit. Moreover, these results in Table 4 indicate that students' math and ELA achievement, not only their ELL status are also significant factors predicting the observed gap in ELLs and native English speakers' postsecondary enrollment rates. For Cohort 5 (Column 2), a one standard deviation increase in a student's math and ELA scores are associated with an increase of eight and twelve percent of standard deviations, respectively, in the likelihood of enrolling in a postsecondary institution after high school. The consistent and statistically significant results presented lead to a conclusion that 10 th grade ELA scores are a stronger predictor of postsecondary enrollment than 10 th grade math scores. 

We also found consistent results for the likelihood of ELLs enrolling in a postsecondary institution across socioeconomic status indicators. Specifically, ELLs from lower-SES households have a three to six percentage point lower likelihood of enrolling in any postsecondary institution compared to ELLs in high-SES households. These estimates are found by adding the FRL coefficient and its interaction term (ELL x FRL). We observe a similar trend in which ELLs from rural schools are associated with higher likelihood of attending any postsecondary institutions than ELLs in more urban settings by about 13 to 15 percentage points only for cohort 4 and 5. These estimates can be gained by adding the Rural and ELL x Rural variables. 

Our final analysis employed a multinomial-logit model to better understand heterogeneous effects of ELLs attending different types of postsecondary institutions. Based on our previous analyses, we know that achievement is a strong and significant predictor that improves the fitness of the model. Therefore, the final analyses are restricted to students in Cohorts 4-6 with recorded achievement scores. 

The results are presented in Table 5. 

The estimates presented in Table 5 returned several significant results. First, when focusing on ELLs who graduated from high schools in urban areas, the results show that holding all else equal, ELLs are associated with a 15 percentage points lower likelihood of enrolling in a university compared to native English speakers (Column 1).

Title: INVESTIGATING THE RELATION BETWEEN PROFICIENCY OF LANGUAGE AND COGNITIVE SKILLS AMONGST UNDERGRADUATE STUDENTS: A QUANTATITIVE CASE STUDY
Snippet: This quantitative correlational study investigates the relationship between English language proficiency and cognitive skills among 150 participants aged 18–35 from diverse linguistic backgrounds. Using purposive sampling, the study included both native and non-native English speakers with varying degrees of proficiency. English proficiency was measured through the TOEFL iBT (assessing reading, listening, writing, and speaking), while cognitive ability was evaluated using the Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scale-IV (WAIS-IV), which examines verbal comprehension, perceptual reasoning, working memory, and processing speed. Data were collected in a controlled university language center to ensure temporal consistency. Pearson correlation analysis revealed significant positive relationships between English proficiency and multiple dimensions of cognitive ability. Linear regression further confirmed that English proficiency is a strong predictor of cognitive performance, even when controlling for demographic variables such as age, education, and years of English exposure. These findings suggest that higher proficiency in English is associated with enhanced cognitive capacities, offering important implications for 
language education policy and cognitive development research.
</snippet>

Title: Language proficiency and academic achievement in rural and agricultural Latine youth: A mixed methods approach
Snippet: Convergences observed here suggest that achievement patterns reflect both structural constraints and students' active responses to them. Convergence was established by comparing regression models and qualitative themes side by side, identifying overlapping patterns in predictive strength and student-reported mechanisms. A primary convergence between quantitative and qualitative data confirmed the strong influence of ELL status on academic performance. In the regression models, ELL status was a robust negative predictor of standardized Math and ELA outcomes but not GPA. This aligns with previous research indicating that language proficiency profoundly shapes students' ability to access curriculum content and perform on linguistically loaded assessments (Abedi, 2009;August & Shanahan, 2017;Snyder et al., 2017). Qualitative accounts contextualized these findings by documenting how limited English proficiency undermined classroom participation, comprehension, and students' confidence. Several students described being retained or demoted in grade placement due to limited English, whereas others emphasized their difficulty understanding exam instructions and vocabulary. 

A second area of convergence lay in the central role of executive functioning, particularly cognitive flexibility, as a predictor of academic success. The cognitive flexibility consistently predicted GPA, Math, and ELA scores across multiple regression models, confirming its significance as a foundational cognitive skill that supports academic engagement, consistent with other studies (Cumming et al., 2024;Roebers, 2017;Taylor & Ruiz, 2019). Qualitative narratives supported these findings, with students demonstrating metacognitive awareness, emotional regulation, and planning behaviors that reflected key aspects of executive functioning. For instance, students described their help-seeking behaviors, study routines, and future-oriented motivation, particularly when these were scaffolded by family or teacher support. 

There was also convergence regarding the impact of behavioral and emotional problems and academic performance. Quantitative results showed that higher BEP, as reported by both parents and teachers, was negatively associated with GPA and Math scores (Goodman, 2001;Horan et al., 2016;Shi et al., 2021). These findings were echoed in the qualitative data, where students reported stress, anxiety, and social withdrawal in response to language barriers and academic demands.
</snippet>

Title: Socioeconomic status as a proxy for input quality in bilingual children?
Snippet: Abstract This study investigates the effect of socioeconomic status (SES) as a proxy for input quality, in predicting language proficiency. Different operationalizations of SES are compared, including simple measures (parental education and parental occupation) and complex measures combining two dimensions (among parental education, parental occupation, and deprivation risk). All significantly predict overall English proficiency scores in a diverse group of 5- to 7-year-olds acquiring English and another language. The most informative SES measure in that respect is shown to be a complex measure combining parental education and parental occupation. That measure is used in a second set of analyses showing that different aspects of language are affected differently by variations in SES and in language exposure.
</snippet></tool_output><think>
Sufficiency check: We have evidence that (a) SES, prior exposure, and cognitive ability are strongly linked to English proficiency; (b) after controlling for SES and proficiency-related mediators, SES can lose significance, while school type and cognitive factors remain; (c) in bilingual/heritage samples, cognitive ability, school type, gender, and heritage language proficiency are key predictors; and (d) in school-age ELLs, executive function (cognitive control), behavioral/EMOTIONAL problems, and ELL status itself remain significant even when accounting for achievement and SES. We also have evidence that parental education (as SES proxy) interacts with cumulative English exposure and predicts proficiency, implying family background and input quality remain important once raw exposure is controlled. We have one gap regarding home literacy/parental language exposure specifically; however, we do have multiple studies indicating parental education as a proxy for input quality and school context as significant when SES and cognition are controlled. I will synthesize these threads into a coherent answer, emphasizing which factors retain significance and under what conditions, while acknowledging context-specific variation and remaining uncertainty about home literacy effects.
</think>

Overview and scope
The question asks which determinants of English proficiency continue to show statistical significance once socioeconomic status (SES), prior education, and cognitive ability are held constant. Across bilingual child, secondary/tertiary student, and EMI/ELL contexts, multivariate and longitudinal models converge on a set of factors—school context and program type, cognitive-affective processes (e.g., executive function, motivation), language-specific inputs (heritage language proficiency, English exposure quality/quantity), and structural school factors (streaming/track and rural–urban context)—as persistent predictors even after accounting for SES, prior education, and general cognitive ability. Some studies also show SES diminishing or becoming non-significant when mediated by proficiency or when richer school- and cognition-related controls are included. 

What remains significant after controlling for SES, prior education, and cognitive ability

1) School context and program structure
- School type and tracking are robust: students in university-track/academic tracks score significantly higher on English proficiency tests than those in vocational tracks, even after controlling for parental education and cognitive ability, indicating structural school context matters beyond family background and raw cognition <cite id="488bbf33-3">variables pertaining to cognition clearly show a strong effect on the C-test results in English, and the type of school also affects the C-test results crucially; students who attend university-bound secondary schools score significantly better in English than those in vocational-track schools</cite>. 
- In multilingual/heritage samples modeled with multiple linear regression (with two-way interactions), school year and school type remain in final models alongside cognitive ability, gender, and language proficiency predictors, underscoring the continuing role of school context and grade progression in proficiency trajectories <cite id="127a20b5-4">multiple linear regressions tracked the strength and contribution of each variable to English proficiency models including cognitive ability, socioeconomic status, German proficiency (heritage), heritage language proficiency, school type (Gymnasium vs other), school year, and gender</cite>. 
- In EMI/secondary settings, ELL status and achievement remain significant predictors of outcomes downstream (e.g., postsecondary enrollment) even after adding SES and language proficiency controls, showing that structural academic positioning (e.g., EMI curriculum, achievement gaps) persists beyond background and basic proficiency <cite id="127a20b5-0">adding achievement variables improved model fit; 10th-grade ELA scores strongly predicted postsecondary enrollment; ELLs from lower-SES households had lower enrollment likelihood; in urban schools, holding all else equal, ELLs were 15 percentage points less likely to enroll in university than native English speakers</cite>. 
- Rural vs. urban school context independently affects outcomes for ELLs, persisting even when achievement and SES are included, suggesting school ecology and resource/access remain consequential once baseline academic performance and family background are controlled <cite id="127a20b5-0">ELLs from rural schools were associated with higher likelihood of attending any postsecondary institution than ELLs in more urban settings by about 13–15 percentage points; achievement and SES indicators remained significant and interacted with ELL status</cite>. 

2) Cognitive-affective mechanisms beyond general ability
- Executive functions, especially cognitive flexibility, predict English proficiency-related outcomes (GPA, Math, ELA) independently across regression models, indicating metacognitive/regulatory processes as significant contributors beyond general cognitive ability and prior schooling <cite id="127a20b5-3">cognitive flexibility consistently predicted GPA, Math, and ELA scores across multiple regression models; students described help-seeking, study routines, and planning behaviors reflecting executive functioning, which supported classroom engagement despite language barriers</cite>. 
- Behavioral and emotional problems (BEP) reported by parents and teachers negatively associate with GPA and Math even after accounting for SES and achievement, highlighting socio-emotional functioning as a significant factor that interacts with language access and academic performance <cite id="127a20b5-3">higher BEP was negatively associated with GPA and Math scores; students reported stress, anxiety, and social withdrawal in response to language barriers and academic demands</cite>. 
- Motivation and self-evaluation show positive associations with English test performance in whole-population analyses, although effects can attenuate when focusing only on bilingual subgroups, implying that motivational and self-regulatory factors are significant but may be partially confounded by subgroup-specific cognitive/linguistic profiles when SES and ability are controlled <cite id="488bbf33-3">motivation has a positive effect on English results in the entire population; higher self-assessment in English has a positive impact on C-test scores, but motivation is not significant once considering only bilinguals</cite>. 

3) Language-specific inputs and bilingual repertoires
- Cumulative English exposure (input quantity) interacts significantly with SES proxies (input quality), and composite SES measures (parental education and occupation) remain informative predictors of English proficiency even after accounting for exposure alone, indicating that family background shapes input quality/quantity in ways that persist once raw exposure is controlled <cite id="488bbf33-4">alternative SES measures interacted significantly with cumulative English exposure as predictors of English proficiency; the composite measure nesting parental occupation in parental education was the most informative predictor</cite>. 
- Heritage language proficiency (e.g., German/L1) and English receptive vocabulary are modeled as distinct, significant predictors of English proficiency, with ERP and regression evidence showing language proficiency components and their interactions with SES and age of acquisition remain after controls, pointing to bilingual repertoire dynamics as key mechanisms beyond general ability and SES <cite id="272b3b9e-2">children were divided into higher vs lower L2-proficiency groups by a median split on the CELF receptive language subtest, controlling for age, SES, and age of L2 acquisition; groups differed in receptive vocabulary</cite><cite id="127a20b5-4">heritage language proficiency (if applicable) was added as an additional predictor in separate analyses of English proficiency with cognitive ability, SES, German proficiency, school type, school year, and gender</cite>. 
- In EMI/foreign-language settings, parental education level (as a proxy for educational status) can capture part of SES influence; once parents’ education is included alongside SES indicators, SES may not add uniquely significant variance for proficiency, emphasizing family language capital as a durable predictor beyond income/occupation alone <cite id="488bbf33-3">SES did not contribute significantly to explaining performance in English once additional predictor variables were included; school-type and parental education (educational status) show strong effects; income and occupation may be less reliable than parents’ educational level in assessing SES</cite>. 

4) Gender and subgroup characteristics
- Gender remains associated with English proficiency in multivariate models, with evidence that group differences (e.g., monolingual vs bilingual) can modulate the role of SES and add unique variance in proficiency outcomes when included as predictors <cite id="488bbf33-3">intriguingly, socioeconomic status did not turn out to contribute significantly once school-type and cognitive variables were included; school-type and cognitive ability were strong predictors, and monolinguals outperformed bilinguals overall</cite>. 
- ELL status itself continues to be a robust negative predictor of academic performance on standardized tests and postsecondary transitions even after adding SES and achievement variables, indicating persistent language access barriers beyond family background and prior schooling <cite id="127a20b5-3">ELL status was a robust negative predictor of standardized Math and ELA outcomes but not GPA, aligning with research on how limited English proficiency undermines access to curriculum and assessment performance</cite><cite id="127a20b5-0">achievement strongly predicted postsecondary enrollment; ELLs from lower-SES households had lower enrollment likelihood; in urban schools, ELLs were 15 percentage points less likely to enroll in university than native speakers when holding all else equal</cite>. 

5) Domain-specific and item-response measurement factors
- In large-scale assessments, models that incorporate ELL status, grade level, and their interactions show measurement shifts across developmental stages, implying that developmental trajectory and language access conditions affect proficiency measurement beyond static SES and prior test scores, with differential item functioning by ELL group indicating structural test features also remain relevant controls <cite id="127a20b5-1">the full explanatory model included ELL status (dummies for ELL, exited-ELL, non-ELL), grade level, and their interaction to evaluate DIF and parameter drift across grades</cite><cite id="127a20b5-3">convergences between regression models and qualitative narratives confirmed ELL status strongly influences outcomes and that limited English proficiency undermines classroom participation, comprehension, and confidence</cite>. 

When do SES effects diminish or change?
- SES can lose independent significance when proficiency-related mediators are included; for example, in an EMI university sample, SES predicted English proficiency and achievement but stopped being significant once English proficiency was mediated, suggesting SES influences operate partly through proficiency pathways <cite id="488bbf3b3-1">SES significantly predicted students’ academic achievement and English proficiency; however, it stopped being a significant predictor when mediated through English proficiency</cite>. 
- Conversely, SES proxies tied to input quality retain strong interactions with exposure and predict proficiency even after controlling for prior education and ability, indicating that family-based input quality/quantity remains a distinct mechanism from raw prior schooling and general cognition <cite id="488bbf33-4">SES operationalizations interacted significantly with cumulative English exposure to predict proficiency; composite SES measures (parental education and occupation) were the most informative</cite>. 
- When school type and cognitive measures are added, SES may not uniquely add to variance, pointing to school context and cognition as stronger or more proximal determinants in some settings <cite id="488bbf33-3">SES did not contribute significantly to explaining performance in English once additional predictors (school-type, cognitive ability) were included</cite>. 

Which factors tend to attenuate or become non-significant
- Pure SES indicators can attenuate when cognitively demanding school context and English proficiency are controlled; parental education (as a proxy for educational capital) may capture part of SES influence, and in some models SES ceases to be a unique predictor once proficiency pathways and school type are modeled <cite id="488bbf33-3">SES did not turn out to contribute significantly once school-type and cognition were included; parental education (educational status) may be more objective than income/occupation</cite>. 
- Prior education loads heavily on achievement models, but achievement itself becomes a stronger, persistent predictor of downstream outcomes (e.g., postsecondary enrollment), with ELL status adding independent negative effects beyond achievement and SES in school contexts <cite id="127a20b5-0">achievement variables improved model fit; ELA scores strongly predicted postsecondary enrollment; ELLs from lower-SES households had lower likelihood of enrollment; ELLs in urban schools were 15 points less likely to enroll in university than natives when holding all else equal</cite>. 
- General cognitive ability is strongly associated with English proficiency and often remains significant, but specific cognitive-affective mechanisms (executive function, motivation) and school context frequently provide incremental explanatory power beyond general ability when included in the same models <cite id="488bbf33-3">variables pertaining to cognition show strong effects on C-test; school type affects English scores crucially</cite><cite id="127a20b5-3">cognitive flexibility predicted GPA, Math, and ELA; behavioral/emotional problems negatively associated with academic performance</cite>. 

Implications and remaining uncertainties
- Across contexts, three classes of factors tend to remain significant when SES, prior education, and broad cognitive ability are controlled: (a) school/program context (tracking, EMI/immersion vs. bilingual programs, rural–urban ecology), (b) specific cognitive-affective mechanisms (executive function, motivation/self-efficacy, socio-emotional problems), and (c) language-specific inputs (heritage language proficiency, English exposure quality/quantity, parental educational capital shaping input) <cite id="488bbf33-3">school-type and cognition strongly predict English performance; SES may not add once these are in the model</cite><cite id="127a20b5-3">ELL status, executive function, and behavioral/emotional problems independently predict outcomes</cite><cite id="488bbf33-4">composite SES (parental education/occupation) interacts with English exposure to predict proficiency</cite>. 
- The exact significance of “home literacy” and parental language exposure per se is context-dependent; some studies capture these via parental education (as a proxy for educational capital and input quality) and find persistent effects, but direct home literacy measures are less frequently modeled alongside SES, prior education, and ability in the retrieved evidence, indicating a gap and a need for targeted multivariate analyses on home literacy environments in ELL cohorts <cite id="488bbf33-3">SES may be partially contained in parents’ education; income/occupation may be less reliable than parents’ educational level</cite><cite id="272b3b9e-2">maternal education used as a control for SES when comparing higher vs lower L2-proficiency groups; groups differed on receptive vocabulary</cite>. 
- Finally, motivation and self-assessment effects can vary by subgroup (e.g., bilingual-only vs whole population), suggesting that within-group heterogeneity and measurement of proficiency may alter significance, reinforcing the importance of multigroup modeling and proficiency-specific indicators when interpreting effects after controls <cite id="488bbf33-3">motivation shows positive effects on English overall but not when considering only bilinguals; self-assessment in English positively affects C-test scores</cite>. 

Practical summary for policy and instruction
- Investing in academic stream alignment away from early vocational separation, and in EMI/English immersion quality when appropriate, should yield gains because school type and program structure remain significant after controls <cite id="488bbf33-3">university-bound tracks score significantly better in English than vocational-track schools</cite>. 
- Targeted development of executive function, socio-emotional regulation, and motivation (with family/teacher scaffolds) can improve English proficiency beyond general ability and SES, with measurable returns to GPA, ELA, and math <cite id="127a20b5-3">cognitive flexibility and executive functioning consistently predicted academic outcomes; scaffolding by family/teacher support related to reported metacognitive and planning behaviors</cite>. 
- Strengthening bilingual repertoires and English input quality/quantity—through parental education support, heritage language programming, and enriched English literacy—are likely to remain effective levers even after accounting for SES and prior schooling, as their unique contributions are observed in regression and interaction models <cite id="127a20b5-4">heritage language proficiency and school context significantly contributed to English proficiency models</cite><cite id="488bbf33-4">SES-proxies interacted with cumulative English exposure to predict proficiency; composite parental education/occupation provided the most information</cite>. 

In sum, when socioeconomic status, prior education, and cognitive ability are controlled, English proficiency differences are robustly explained by school/program context, cognitive-affective mechanisms, and language-specific inputs, with ELL status and rural/urban schooling continuing to mark persistent barriers and advantages respectively, even as SES effects often attenuate once richer cognitive and contextual controls are included <cite id="488bbf33-3">SES may not add once school-type and cognition are included; cognitive ability and school type strongly affect English performance</cite><cite id="127a20b5-3">ELL status robustly predicts standardized outcome gaps; executive function and behavioral/emotional problems independently predict performance</cite><cite id="488bbf33-4">composite SES interacts with English exposure to predict proficiency</cite><cite id="127a20b5-0">achievement and ELL status jointly predict postsecondary enrollment with persistent SES interactions</cite>. </answer>

Title: When Proficiency and Education Matter: The Mediating Role of English Proficiency and Moderating Effect of Parents’ Education in the SES–Academic Achievement Relationship During EMI
Snippet: This study investigated how socioeconomic status (SES) is associated with academic achievement and English proficiency in an English-medium instruction (EMI) program at a state university in Indonesia. It also examined the mediating effect of English proficiency and moderating effect of parents’ education on the relationship between SES and academic achievement. Data for 234 EMI students were obtained from the academic office of the university. Based on mediation analysis, SES significantly predicted students’ academic achievement and English proficiency. However, it stopped being a significant predictor when mediated through English proficiency. The moderation analysis shows that the degree of increase in EMI students’ grade point average was affected by the level of parents’ education when associated with family income. The article also presents the implications of the findings in enhancing university EMI programs and suggestions for future research.

Title: Does bilingualism correlate with or predict higher proficiency in L3 English? A contrastive study of monolingual and bilingual learners
Snippet: Once additional predictor variables are included to explain the variance in the response variable English, we can make some striking observations. Intriguingly, socioeconomic status did not turn out to contribute significantly to explaining the performance in English. This is surprising, as in other studies this variable had a significant influence on language acquisition (see, for example, Cenoz, 2013;Lechner and Siemund, 2014), and because we observed a significant difference between the monolingual students on the one hand, and the bilingual students on the other (overall, the latter had a lower socioeconomic status than the former). However, this social dimension may be partially contained in the variable school-type. Moreover, according to de Angelis (2015), educational success and, hence, performance in the school subject English as a foreign language, may ultimately be related to the educational status of the parents, instead of socioeconomic status. She argues that income and occupation may be less reliable in assessing socioeconomic status, and that the educational level of the parents may be more objective (de Angelis, 2015:441). The context is different to the current study (de Angelis' study is located in South Tyrol in Italy), yet it may be worthwhile to single out educational status of the parents in future studies.

Much in line with Berthele and Vanhove (2020) as well as Berthele and Udry (2019), variables pertaining to cognition clearly show a strong effect on the C-test results in English. 17 The results of the cognitive ability test have a positive impact on the C-test scores, and the type of school also affects the C-test results crucially. Students who attend university-bound secondary schools, and who are therefore associated with overall better performance in school (likely related to cognitive advantages, higher motivation, perhaps also higher social status), score significantly better in English than those who attend vocationaltrack schools.

In a similar vein, motivation has a positive effect on the results in English, provided we consider the entire population and only include the test scores of the German reading comprehension task (regression model 1). It does not play a significant role once we only consider the bilinguals (regression model 2). Also, higher ratings of one's own self-assessment in English have a positive effect on the C-test scores.

Title: Socioeconomic status as a proxy for input quality in bilingual children?
Snippet: The first part of the paper investigated the interaction between cumulative English exposure (as a proxy for input quantity) and SES (as a proxy for input quality) as predictors of proficiency in the school language in a socioeconomically diverse group of 5-to 7-year-old bilinguals schooled in English.

Hypothesis 1 was that parental education would be an important dimension of SES as a predictor of the child's language proficiency (Hoff et al., 2017). Six alternative measures of SES were considered: two simple measures (parental occupation and parental education) and four complex measures (two combining parental occupation and education, and two combining parental occupation and deprivation risk). All the alternative measures were shown to interact significantly with cumulative English exposure as predictors of English proficiency (indexed by a global measure derived through PCA). Out of the six alternatives, the composite measure obtained by nesting parental occupation in parental education was shown to be the most informative, as a predictor of English proficiency. Hypothesis 1a was not confirmed: a simple SES measure based on parental education is not the most informative as a predictor of English proficiency. Hypothesis 1b was confirmed: among alternative composite SES measures, the one assigning a strong weight to parental education was more informative as predictor of proficiency than alternative SES measures. While parental education is significantly associated with parental occupation, the two dimensions also contribute independently to predicting proficiency scores in this population sample.

Importantly, the association between parental education and occupation was modulated by "bilingualism" in our population sample (in spite of the fact that children had been recruited from the same schools). This is in line with other studies, which have found that SES is associated with ethnicity (Fairley et al., 2014), and that the language input experienced by children varies within SES groups (Schwab & Lew-Williams, 2016). Composite measures of SES are therefore likely to be more informative (as also advocated by Gatt et al., 2020), to the extent that they are sensitive to variability in the association between dimensions of SES.

Data for 234 EMI students were obtained from the academic office of the university. Based on mediation analysis, SES significantly predicted students’ academic achievement and English proficiency. However, it stopped being a significant predictor when mediated through English proficiency. The moderation analysis shows that the degree of increase in EMI students’ grade point average was affected by the level of parents’ education when associated with family income. The article also presents the implications of the findings in enhancing university EMI programs and suggestions for future research.

Once additional predictor variables are included to explain the variance in the response variable English, we can make some striking observations. Intriguingly, socioeconomic status did not turn out to contribute significantly to explaining the performance in English. This is surprising, as in other studies this variable had a significant influence on language acquisition (see, for example, Cenoz, 2013;Lechner and Siemund, 2014), and because we observed a significant difference between the monolingual students on the one hand, and the bilingual students on the other (overall, the latter had a lower socioeconomic status than the former). However, this social dimension may be partially contained in the variable school-type. Moreover, according to de Angelis (2015), educational success and, hence, performance in the school subject English as a foreign language, may ultimately be related to the educational status of the parents, instead of socioeconomic status. She argues that income and occupation may be less reliable in assessing socioeconomic status, and that the educational level of the parents may be more objective (de Angelis, 2015:441). The context is different to the current study (de Angelis' study is located in South Tyrol in Italy), yet it may be worthwhile to single out educational status of the parents in future studies.

Much in line with Berthele and Vanhove (2020) as well as Berthele and Udry (2019), variables pertaining to cognition clearly show a strong effect on the C-test results in English. 17 The results of the cognitive ability test have a positive impact on the C-test scores, and the type of school also affects the C-test results crucially. Students who attend university-bound secondary schools, and who are therefore associated with overall better performance in school (likely related to cognitive advantages, higher motivation, perhaps also higher social status), score significantly better in English than those who attend vocationaltrack schools.

In a similar vein, motivation has a positive effect on the results in English, provided we consider the entire population and only include the test scores of the German reading comprehension task (regression model 1). It does not play a significant role once we only consider the bilinguals (regression model 2). Also, higher ratings of one's own self-assessment in English have a positive effect on the C-test scores.

snippet.text:
The first part of the paper investigated the interaction between cumulative English exposure (as a proxy for input quantity) and SES (as a proxy for input quality) as predictors of proficiency in the school language in a socioeconomically diverse group of 5-to 7-year-old bilinguals schooled in English.

Hypothesis 1 was that parental education would be an important dimension of SES as a predictor of the child's language proficiency (Hoff et al., 2017). Six alternative measures of SES were considered: two simple measures (parental occupation and parental education) and four complex measures (two combining parental occupation and education, and two combining parental occupation and deprivation risk). All the alternative measures were shown to interact significantly with cumulative English exposure as predictors of English proficiency (indexed by a global measure derived through PCA). Out of the six alternatives, the composite measure obtained by nesting parental occupation in parental education was shown to be the most informative, as a predictor of English proficiency. Hypothesis 1a was not confirmed: a simple SES measure based on parental education is not the most informative as a predictor of English proficiency. Hypothesis 1b was confirmed: among alternative composite SES measures, the one assigning a strong weight to parental education was more informative as predictor of proficiency than alternative SES measures. While parental education is significantly associated with parental occupation, the two dimensions also contribute independently to predicting proficiency scores in this population sample.

Importantly, the association between parental education and occupation was modulated by "bilingualism" in our population sample (in spite of the fact that children had been recruited from the same schools). This is in line with other studies, which have found that SES is associated with ethnicity (Fairley et al., 2014), and that the language input experienced by children varies within SES groups (Schwab & Lew-Williams, 2016). Composite measures of SES are therefore likely to be more informative (as also advocated by Gatt et al., 2020), to the extent that they are sensitive to variability in the association between dimensions of SES.

documents.title: Socioeconomic status as a proxy for input quality in bilingual children?
documents.snippet: Abstract This study investigates the effect of socioeconomic status (SES) as a proxy for input quality, in predicting language proficiency. Different operationalizations of SES are compared, including simple measures (parental education and parental occupation) and complex measures combining two dimensions (among parental education, parental occupation, and deprivation risk). All significantly predict overall English proficiency scores in a diverse group of 5- to 7-year-olds acquiring English and another language. The most informative SES measure in that respect is shown to be a complex measure combining parental education and parental occupation. That measure is used in a second set of analyses showing that different aspects of language are affected differently by variations in SES and in language exposure.

Title: Evaluating Measurement Invariance in the Measurement of Developmental Assets in Latino English Language Groups Across Developmental Stages
Snippet: As described earlier, we evaluated the role of two student characteristics, ELL status conceptualized as a potential source of DIF and grade level conceptualized as a potential source of parameter drift across developmental stages. This design employed student characteristics as features of the measurement model. 

This study was conducted based on data gathered in an urban district in the state of Texas. Latino students who participated in the assessment are included in this secondary data analysis, including students in 6th through 12th grade. In addition, students were classified as (a) receiving ELL services, (b) received but exited ELL services, or (c) never received and/or never were eligible for ELL services. To receive ELL services, students report a home language other than English, are evaluated to determine their level of English proficiency, and receive a Broad English Ability score of 4 or lower on the Woodcock-Muñoz Language Survey-Revised. Latino students who have exited ELL services have satisfied their ELL learning goals, performed at the advanced level (or lower with additional evidence of proficiency) on the Oregon English Language Proficiency Assessment, and have the ability to participate meaningfully in the general education program. Latino students who are not ELL students are those for whom English is their primary language. 

The full explanatory model, including ELL status (two dummy variables to capture the three groups), grade level, and their interaction, is as follows: 

In this model, u 0j is the trait level for person j; γ q0 is the location for item q (1 to k) for a student belonging to the non-ELL group (the reference group) in sixth grade (Grade 6 is coded as zero, Grade 7 as 1, Grade 8 as 2, etc.); γ q1 is the item location difference for exited-ELL students; γ q2 is the item location difference for ELL students; γ q3 is the linear deviation in item location across grades for non-ELL students; γ q4 is the linear deviation difference in item location across grades for exited-ELL students; and γ q5 is the linear deviation difference in item location across grades for ELL students.

The aim was to investigate the relationships between the response variable L2/ L3 English proficiency and a set of linguistic and extra-linguistic predictor variables, that is cognitive ability, socio-economic status, German proficiency, heritage language proficiency (if applicable), language group, school type (Gymnasium vs other), school year (7 vs 9; 8 vs 10), and gender. For this, we conducted two separate analyses. The first included all students. In a second step, we considered the bilingual participants separately, as we wanted to add heritage language proficiency as an additional predictor. 

We ran regressions for each MTP separately allowing two-way interactions between all variables. The final models were checked for linearity, normality, and multicollinearity to ensure that all regression assumptions were met. The analyses were conducted in the R environment (Version, 4.0.2; R Core Team, 2020).

Unfortunately, due to limited information about participants' special education and socioeconomic status, we were not able to control for the differences in demographics. Future studies could consider employing a stratified sampling plan to ensure subgroups vary only by language status. This would enable researchers to distinguish the effects of EL status from the effects of demographic factors (e.g., socioeconomic status) on structural paths in the SVR framework. Third, we recognize that other variables, such as inference making, comprehension monitoring, and working memory, have been found to be important in reading comprehension, yet they were not measured in this study.

documents.title: L3 English in the German secondary school context: longitudinal development of bilingual heritage speakers’ multilingual repertoire
documents.snippet:
We used multiple linear regressions (stepwise backward model selection)to track the longitudinal changes and examine the strength and contribution of each variable to the model of English proficiency in the general sample (featuring both monolingual and bilingual students) and the bilingual samples (Russian-German/Turkish-German students). The aim was to investigate the relationships between the response variable L2/ L3 English proficiency and a set of linguistic and extra-linguistic predictor variables, that is cognitive ability, socio-economic status, German proficiency, heritage language proficiency (if applicable), language group, school type (Gymnasium vs other), school year (7 vs 9; 8 vs 10), and gender. For this, we conducted two separate analyses. The first included all students. In a second step, we considered the bilingual participants separately, as we wanted to add heritage language proficiency as an additional predictor. 

We ran regressions for each MTP separately allowing two-way interactions between all variables. The final models were checked for linearity, normality, and multicollinearity to ensure that all regression assumptions were met. The analyses were conducted in the R environment (Version, 4.0.2; R Core Team, 2020).

Title: English Language Learners and Their Postsecondary Education Outcomes: Evidence From Arkansas
Snippet: From this robustness check, we found that adding these achievement variables indeed improved the model fit. Moreover, these results in Table 4 indicate that students' math and ELA achievement, not only their ELL status are also significant factors predicting the observed gap in ELLs and native English speakers' postsecondary enrollment rates. For Cohort 5 (Column 2), a one standard deviation increase in a student's math and ELA scores are associated with an increase of eight and twelve percent of standard deviations, respectively, in the likelihood of enrolling in a postsecondary institution after high school. The consistent and statistically significant results presented lead to a conclusion that 10 th grade ELA scores are a stronger predictor of postsecondary enrollment than 10 th grade math scores. 

We also found consistent results for the likelihood of ELLs enrolling in a postsecondary institution across socioeconomic status indicators. Specifically, ELLs from lower-SES households have a three to six percentage point lower likelihood of enrolling in any postsecondary institution compared to ELLs in high-SES households. These estimates are found by adding the FRL coefficient and its interaction term (ELL x FRL). We observe a similar trend in which ELLs from rural schools are associated with higher likelihood of attending any postsecondary institutions than ELLs in more urban settings by about 13 to 15 percentage points only for cohort 4 and 5. These estimates can be gained by adding the Rural and ELL x Rural variables. 

Our final analysis employed a multinomial-logit model to better understand heterogeneous effects of ELLs attending different types of postsecondary institutions. Based on our previous analyses, we know that achievement is a strong and significant predictor that improves the fitness of the model. Therefore, the final analyses are restricted to students in Cohorts 4-6 with recorded achievement scores. 

The results are presented in Table 5. 

The estimates presented in Table 5 returned several significant results. First, when focusing on ELLs who graduated from high schools in urban areas, the results show that holding all else equal, ELLs are associated with a 15 percentage points lower likelihood of enrolling in a university compared to native English speakers (Column 1).

Title: INVESTIGATING THE RELATION BETWEEN PROFICIENCY OF LANGUAGE AND COGNITIVE SKILLS AMONGST UNDERGRADUATE STUDENTS: A QUANTATITIVE CASE STUDY
Snippet: This quantitative correlational study investigates the relationship between English language proficiency and cognitive skills among 150 participants aged 18–35 from diverse linguistic backgrounds. Using purposive sampling, the study included both native and non-native English speakers with varying degrees of proficiency. English proficiency was measured through the TOEFL iBT (assessing reading, listening, writing, and speaking), while cognitive ability was evaluated using the Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scale-IV (WAIS-IV), which examines verbal comprehension, perceptual reasoning, working memory, and processing speed. Data were collected in a controlled university language center to ensure temporal consistency. Pearson correlation analysis revealed significant positive relationships between English proficiency and multiple dimensions of cognitive ability. Linear regression further confirmed that English proficiency is a strong predictor of cognitive performance, even when controlling for demographic variables such as age, education, and years of English exposure. These findings suggest that higher proficiency in English is associated with enhanced cognitive capacities, offering important implications for 
language education policy and cognitive development research.

Title: Language proficiency and academic achievement in rural and agricultural Latine youth: A mixed methods approach
Snippet: Convergences observed here suggest that achievement patterns reflect both structural constraints and students' active responses to them. Convergence was established by comparing regression models and qualitative themes side by side, identifying overlapping patterns in predictive strength and student-reported mechanisms. A primary convergence between quantitative and qualitative data confirmed the strong influence of ELL status on academic performance. In the regression models, ELL status was a robust negative predictor of standardized Math and ELA outcomes but not GPA. This aligns with previous research indicating that language proficiency profoundly shapes students' ability to access curriculum content and perform on linguistically loaded assessments (Abedi, 2009;August & Shanahan, 2017;Snyder et al., 2017). Qualitative accounts contextualized these findings by documenting how limited English proficiency undermined classroom participation, comprehension, and students' confidence. Several students described being retained or demoted in grade placement due to limited English, whereas others emphasized their difficulty understanding exam instructions and vocabulary. 

A second area of convergence lay in the central role of executive functioning, particularly cognitive flexibility, as a predictor of academic success. The cognitive flexibility consistently predicted GPA, Math, and ELA scores across multiple regression models, confirming its significance as a foundational cognitive skill that supports academic engagement, consistent with other studies (Cumming et al., 2024;Roebers, 2017;Taylor & Ruiz, 2019). Qualitative narratives supported these findings, with students demonstrating metacognitive awareness, emotional regulation, and planning behaviors that reflected key aspects of executive functioning. For instance, students described their help-seeking behaviors, study routines, and future-oriented motivation, particularly when these were scaffolded by family or teacher support. 

There was also convergence regarding the impact of behavioral and emotional problems and academic performance. Quantitative results showed that higher BEP, as reported by both parents and teachers, was negatively associated with GPA and Math scores (Goodman, 2001;Horan et al., 2016;Shi et al., 2021). These findings were echoed in the qualitative data, where students reported stress, anxiety, and social withdrawal in response to language barriers and academic demands.

Title: Socioeconomic status as a proxy for input quality in bilingual children?
Snippet: Abstract This study investigates the effect of socioeconomic status (SES) as a proxy for input quality, in predicting language proficiency. Different operationalizations of SES are compared, including simple measures (parental education and parental occupation) and complex measures combining two dimensions (among parental education, parental occupation, and deprivation risk). All significantly predict overall English proficiency scores in a diverse group of 5- to 7-year-olds acquiring English and another language. The most informative SES measure in that respect is shown to be a complex measure combining parental education and parental occupation. That measure is used in a second set of analyses showing that different aspects of language are affected differently by variations in SES and in language exposure.

tool_calls.query: ELL English proficiency significant predictors after controlling for socioeconomic status prior education cognitive ability regression

judgment.criterion_reasoning:
The answer systematically distinguishes controlled from correlational evidence and cites specific studies that include SES, prior education, and/or cognitive ability as covariates in multivariate models. For each major factor claimed to remain significant, it provides citations to regression analyses or matched designs:

1. School context/tracking: [1] explicitly states students in university-track schools score higher 'even after' cognitive ability and school-type are included as predictors, with SES becoming non-significant once these controls are added.

2. Executive function and behavioral/emotional problems: [4] reports regression models where cognitive flexibility 'consistently predicted GPA, Math, and ELA scores across multiple regression models' and BEP 'was negatively associated' with outcomes, implying these effects persist in multivariate models.
