attempts.answer:
Below is an evidence-based explanation of why extensive reading (ER) improves English proficiency more for some students than others, organized by mechanisms and contextual moderators that create heterogeneity.

Summary of average effects and moderators
- Across meta-analyses, ER improves multiple language domains—reading speed/comprehension, vocabulary, grammar, motivation, speaking, and writing—with medium-to-large effects compared to control conditions, and especially when programs are well-structured and aligned to learners’ levels and interests. <cite id="1ab583e4-0">Effects of ER span decoding/fluency, grammar, reading comprehension, motivation, speaking, vocabulary, and writing, with moderators including learner type, L1, educational level, and intervention features such as text limitation, help with text selection, accountability, instruction during ER, rewards, digital support, provision of books, graded readers, medium, and duration</cite> <cite id="1ab583e4-1">ER programs show positive impacts on reading proficiency (d≈0.71 overall), outperforming controls (d≈0.46); effects vary by moderators—larger for adults, in EFL settings, with web texts, and when ER is part of a course or extracurricular activity, though overrepresentation of certain study types warrants caution</cite>.
- Program design features and dose matter. ER programs that incorporate accountability (logs, monitoring), guidance (selection help, pre-/during-reading instruction), rewards, and steady access to books at scale produce stronger gains than unstructured free reading. <cite id="1ab583e4-0">Intervention moderators consistently highlight text limitation, help with text selection, accountability, instructional support before/during ER, rewards, digital support, home book provision, graded readers, and duration as features linked to success</cite> <cite id="10663c84-3">Sustaining ER requires highly self-motivated students; without assessment or structure, outcomes may not be realized, and length of texts can frustrate unmotivated learners</cite>.
- Baseline proficiency and age interact with benefits. Meta-analytic syntheses suggest older learners and those with longer instruction periods tend to show larger gains, while subgroup differences can be attenuated by sampling imbalances. <cite id="1ab583e4-1">Effects increase with age and longer instruction periods, though meta-analytic comparisons caution that effects in some subgroups (e.g., adults, EFL, web texts) may reflect overrepresentation</cite>.

Mechanisms that drive heterogeneous responsiveness

1) Comprehensible input, vocabulary coverage, and exposure frequency
- ER works when texts are sufficiently comprehensible and provide repeated, spaced encounters with new words in rich contexts; this boosts vocabulary growth, which in turn raises comprehension and fluency. <cite id="f5ea37ef-0">Vocabulary acquisition depends on input and repeated encounters; texts for vocabulary growth should have ≤5% unknown tokens (with ≥1–2% target), enabling learners to guess from context and accumulate long-term retention via spaced repetition on the order of 6–16 encounters, with recent work suggesting ≥10 high-quality encounters</cite> <cite id="f5ea37ef-2">Reviews converge on lexical coverage, incidental vs. direct vocabulary learning, rate of new word learning from graded readers, and the role of instructional support for lexis in driving reading comprehension</cite>.
- Graded readers can optimize coverage and motivation; however, their simplicity can also limit exposure to lower-frequency academic vocabulary, making unsupervised graded reading alone insufficient for complex text comprehension without scaffolding. <cite id="f5ea37ef-1">Graded readers increase vocabulary, fluency, and motivation through multiple exposures and reinforcement of known lexicon</cite> <cite id="f5ea37ef-3">Graded readers often target ~98% comprehensible input (≈2 unknowns/page), but critics argue they expose learners to too few lower-frequency terms, requiring impractically large quantities for incidental gains and insufficient input for complex texts without additional instruction</cite>.
- Responsiveness varies by how well a student’s reading level and interests align to text difficulty and dose. Students who read more books in ER programs show larger comprehension gains, indicating a dose-response pattern that depends on sustained motivation and access. <cite id="10663c84-0">Students who read more books in an ER program scored significantly higher on reading comprehension than peers who read fewer books, supporting a dose–response</cite> <cite id="10663c84-2">ER emphasizes i–1 to i-level texts for comfort and fluency, with learners abandoning uninteresting or too-difficult materials; motivation and interest are central to maintaining sufficient dose</cite>.

2) Strategy repertoire, metacognition, and prior content knowledge
- ER often co-trains strategies (e.g., inference, simplification, connecting to prior knowledge), which mediate comprehension and transfer to independent reading. Students who actively use strategies and connect text to experience show higher comprehension and fluency; those with weaker strategy use lag behind. <cite id="10663c84-4">Participants’ reading logs showed wide text variety, with prior or content knowledge aiding later comprehension; prior knowledge significantly contributes to reading comprehension and can offset linguistic deficiencies</cite> <cite id="f5ea37ef-4">Successful readers relate real-world experiences and use simplification strategies and connections to prior knowledge; unsuccessful readers get bogged down by word-by-word decoding and lack of contextual knowledge</cite>.
- Baseline cognitive and executive resources shape how ER texts are processed. Learners with stronger executive function (EF) show better reading performance across L1 and L2; SES-related advantages in EF can indirectly amplify ER gains by improving comprehension and text integration. <cite id="1ab583e4-3">Executive function uniquely predicts L1 and L2 reading comprehension and mediates SES effects; SES directly predicts L2 reading comprehension and its indirect path increases with EF, with EF effects remaining after age control</cite>.
- Affective states and mind-wandering modulate learning during reading-intensive interventions; these effects generalize to ER-like settings. Students with higher anxiety or mind-wandering can benefit from structured, paced digital ER (suggesting scaffolding helps regulate off-task thoughts), whereas English learners may respond less well to certain ER formats than monolingual peers, highlighting cultural/language-status contingencies. <cite id="1ab583e4-4">Anxiety, mind-wandering, and language status moderated benefits of a computerized inferential reading intervention; a teacher-led version showed no moderation, underscoring how student and instructional features shape differential response</cite>.

3) Output- and accountability-driven consolidation
- When ER is coupled with low-stakes output (e.g., reading logs, summaries, dictogloss), accountability cues increase attention and memory consolidation. <cite id="10663c84-0">ER programs that incorporated graded readers outperformed traditional close-reading instruction, with larger gains accompanying higher book counts</cite> <cite id="10663c84-3">An extended reading approach with short quizzes improved reading proficiency over classroom-only intensive reading, suggesting that manageable text length plus comprehension checks supported less-motivated intermediate learners</cite>.
- Writing and spelling often improve via ER due to repeated exposure to cohesive structures and discourse patterns, which learners can reimagine in short outputs; responsiveness varies with initial writing proficiency and willingness to produce. <cite id="10663c84-1">Writing and spelling gains have been reported alongside ER use, with learners increasing strategy use, speed, comprehension, attitude, and motivation when texts are matched to ability</cite>.

Who benefits more—and why—and when benefits are smaller or null

- Older, more instructed learners and in EFL contexts: ER effects tend to be larger for adults and in EFL settings, possibly due to greater autonomy, clearer curricular alignment, and sustained, course-integrated accountability. <cite id="1ab583e4-1">Effects were larger for adults and in EFL settings, with course-integrated ER outperforming extracurricular or poorly supported variants after publication-year adjustments</cite>.
- High-dose, well-matched texts with support: Students who complete more books, have access to leveled libraries, and receive guidance on selection and monitoring show larger gains; unmotivated or unsupported learners plateau or regress. <cite id="10663c84-0">More books read correlated with higher comprehension</cite> <cite id="10663c84-2">Students should read texts of i–1/i-level of interest; traditional ER without assessment can discourage unmotivated learners</cite> <cite id="10663c84-3">Without structure, less-motivated learners may avoid longer texts; extended reading with short quizzes improved outcomes over intensive-only classes</cite>.
- Strong EF and prior knowledge: Learners with higher EF and stronger background knowledge benefit more because they integrate new lexical items into schema and sustain on-task behavior; SES-linked EF advantages can widen ER-driven proficiency gaps unless programs explicitly scaffold schema and metacognition. <cite id="1ab583e4-3">EF uniquely predicts reading abilities and mediates SES effects on L2 reading; SES directly predicts L2 reading comprehension</cite> <cite id="10663c84-4">Prior knowledge enhances comprehension and can compensate for linguistic deficiencies</cite>.
- Motivation, autonomy, and affect: Intrinsically motivated students, especially those with high interest in chosen texts, show larger gains; anxiety and mind-wandering reduce benefits unless addressed by structured scaffolds. <cite id="10663c84-2">Choice at comfortable difficulty is recommended to sustain pleasure and fluency; abandoning uninteresting texts prevents demotivation</cite> <cite id="1ab583e4-4">Anxiety and mind-wandering moderated ER-like intervention outcomes; structured formats helped, while English learner status reduced benefit in one condition</cite>.
- Program fit and materials: Overly simplified graded readers can limit academic vocabulary exposure without additional support; authentic but too-difficult texts induce decoding focus and demotivation. Students for whom English background knowledge and academic lexicon are weak may need explicit vocabulary and discourse scaffolds to realize ER gains. <cite id="f5ea37ef-3">Graded reading alone may underexpose learners to lower-frequency academic vocabulary; unsupervised reading may be insufficient for complex texts</cite> <cite id="10663c84-2">Authentic texts that are too difficult push students back into decoding and dictionary reliance; gradual “laddering” up difficulty and following interest mitigate this</cite>.

Failure modes and equity considerations
- Misaligned difficulty and low interest reduce fluency practice and demotivate learners, blunting gains; without accountability, dose falls and benefits diminish. <cite id="10663c84-2">Reading below level for pleasure without monitoring can collapse into inefficient decoding; ER aims to keep students in their comfort zone and follow interest to avoid discouragement</cite> <cite id="10663c84-3">Unmotivated students often disengage from long texts without assessment or manageable chunks</cite>.
- Overreliance on graded readers without scaffolding for academic vocabulary and inference can leave lower-SES or lower-proficiency learners with ceiling effects, as exposure to high-frequency lists alone may not build the lexicon and discourse competence needed for complex texts. <cite id="f5ea37ef-3">Graded readers may not supply enough lower-frequency vocabulary for complex texts without additional instruction</cite>.
- Language-status and affective contingencies can accentuate disparities. English learners may gain less from certain technology-mediated ER formats than peers in supportive, teacher-led models; anxiety and mind-wandering further depress responsiveness, indicating a need for targeted supports. <cite id="1ab583e4-4">English learners benefited less from a computer-led intervention; anxiety and mind-wandering moderated gains, whereas teacher-led instruction showed no moderation</cite>.
- Measured heterogeneity sometimes reflects sampling and methodological imbalances; recent-year, EFL, adult, and web-based ER studies dominate literature, complicating simple subgroup comparisons. <cite id="1ab583e4-1">Moderator patterns (e.g., larger effects in EFL, adults, web texts, course-integrated programs) may reflect overrepresentation of specific study types and publication-year inflation, warranting caution in subgroup claims</cite>.

Practical levers to reduce heterogeneity and widen high-end gains
- Calibrate difficulty and dose: Use leveled books with 95/1–2% unknown-token guidelines; ensure ≥10 high-quality encounters for new words; track and adjust reading logs to maintain interest and manageable length. <cite id="f5ea37ef-0">Target ≤5% unknown tokens with ≥1–2% intentional new vocabulary, and provide repeated, spaced encounters for durable learning</cite> <cite id="f5ea37ef-3">Design for ~98% comprehensible input (~2 unknowns/page) while supplementing lower-frequency vocabulary</cite>.
- Add scaffolds that convert input to output: brief daily summaries, dictogloss, reading journals tied to formative feedback, and periodic quizzes to create accountability without undermining pleasure. <cite id="10663c84-3">Short weekly quizzes improved proficiency beyond intensive-only classes and supported less-motivated students</cite> <cite id="10663c84-0">Accountability and dose (more books read) correlated with higher comprehension</cite>.
- Build schema and strategy explicitly: teach inference, activation of prior knowledge, and simplification strategies; integrate content-focused pre-reading to connect new texts to learners’ experiences. <cite id="10663c84-4">Connecting real-world knowledge and using simplification/inference strategies is characteristic of successful readers; instruction in strategies can move partly/unsusccessful readers toward proficiency</cite>.
- Address EF and affect: embed brief self-regulation routines (planning–monitoring–reflecting), provide structured pacing, and offer choices to regulate mind-wandering and anxiety; for English learners, add bilingual support and culturally responsive texts. <cite id="1ab583e4-4">Structured formats helped students with higher anxiety and mind-wandering; EL status reduced benefits in one condition, underscoring the need for tailored supports</cite> <cite id="1ab583e4-3">EF uniquely predicts reading success; SES advantages via EF can indirectly shape ER responsiveness</cite>.
- Align to curriculum and assessment: integrate ER with writing tasks and speaking presentations; time ER during class and include low-stakes accountability to ensure exposure translates into curricular outcomes. <cite id="1ab583e4-1">ER integrated into courses shows larger effects than purely extracurricular, ungraded versions</cite> <cite id="10663c84-1">ER improves writing and comprehension when texts are matched to ability and sustained</cite>.

Putting it together: a mechanistic map of heterogeneity
- ER improves proficiency by increasing lexical coverage and repetition (vocabulary), building fluency and comprehension through comfortable, high-interest dose, and expanding background knowledge that supports inference; these gains are mediated by strategy use and EF resources, and amplified by structured accountability and output tasks. <cite id="f5ea37ef-0">Vocabulary growth depends on sufficient, repeated, and spaced encounters with comprehensible input</cite> <cite id="10663c84-4">Prior knowledge and strategy use enhance comprehension and can compensate for linguistic deficiencies</cite> <cite id="10663c84-3">Accountability via short quizzes improved outcomes over intensive-only classes</cite>.
- Responsiveness varies because learners differ in baseline vocabulary, EF, motivation, strategy knowledge, and prior content domains; instructional fit (difficulty, interest, autonomy supports, scaffolds) determines whether input converts into durable gains. <cite id="1ab583e4-0">Learner, intervention, and study-level moderators systematically shape ER outcomes</cite> <cite id="1ab583e4-1">Adults, EFL contexts, web texts, and course-integrated ER show larger effects on average, with cautions on sampling</cite> <cite id="f5ea37ef-3">Graded readers can underexpose learners to academic vocabulary without additional scaffolding</cite>.
- Programs that optimize comprehensible input, strategy scaffolding, accountable output, and culturally responsive materials will narrow the ER response gap by supporting the mechanisms that underlie large gains for high-SES, motivated, and higher-proficiency students, while also unlocking growth among lower-SES and lower-proficiency learners who need explicit supports to overcome EF, vocabulary, and affective barriers. <cite id="1ab583e4-3">SES advantages operate partly via EF; targeted EF and schema supports can make ER benefits more equitable</cite> <cite id="10663c84-4">Reading logs and content-knowledge activation can raise comprehension and close gaps</cite>.

Limitations and next steps
- Some reported moderator effects reflect publication and sampling biases; triangulation across classroom, web-based, and long-term implementations is needed to isolate true heterogeneity mechanisms. <cite id="1ab583e4-1">Effect sizes may be inflated and subgroups overrepresented; caution is warranted in subgroup interpretations</cite>.
- Direct mediation tests linking specific ER features to vocabulary growth, strategy gains, and proficiency over time remain scarce; randomized studies that measure encounters, dictionary use, strategy use, and EF/affect trajectories alongside proficiency would sharpen causal inferences. <cite id="1ab583e4-0">Meta-analytic moderators identify candidate mechanisms, but causal mediation within ER programs is under-tested</cite>.

In sum, ER’s uneven effects arise from differential access to effective comprehensible input, variability in learners’ cognitive-affective resources and strategy repertoires, and differences in program fit and accountability. Closing the gap requires calibrating difficulty and dose to interest, adding structured output and strategy scaffolds, and explicitly supporting EF and background knowledge—especially for learners who face vocabulary, motivation, and affective barriers without tailored interventions. <cite id="f5ea37ef-0">Vocabulary coverage, repetition, and spaced exposure</cite> <cite id="10663c84-0">Dose-response with more books read</cite> <cite id="10663c84-2">Comfort-zone text selection and interest</cite> <cite id="1ab583e4-1">Course-integrated and well-supported ER</cite> <cite id="1ab583e4-3">EF and SES pathways to reading success</cite> <cite id="1ab583e4-4">Affective and language-status contingencies</cite>.

Title: Learning a Language Through Reading: A Meta-analysis of Studies on the Effects of Extensive Reading on Second and Foreign Language Learning
Snippet: A meta-analysis by Nakanishi (2015) of 34 pretest-posttest comparisons, including 18 experimental vs. control group studies, showed that extensive reading is effective in promoting second language learners' reading proficiency, including reading speed, reading comprehension, vocabulary, and grammar; learners in ER programs scored better on posttests compared to pretests (d = 0.71) and outperformed learners in control groups (d = 0.46). Nakanishi additionally tested whether intervention effects were affected by learners' age and length of instruction. His conclusions were ambivalent: he suggested that "the effect of extensive reading increases with older participants" (p. 26) and that "longer length of instruction period could improve students' proficiency in English" (p. 27), but at the same time had to conclude there were no statistically significant differences among subgroups. A meta-analysis by Jeon and Day (2016) of 51 experimental vs. control group studies and 20 pre-post design studies revealed a positive effect of extensive reading on learners' reading proficiency, including reading rate, reading comprehension, and vocabulary; learners in ER programs scored better on posttests than pretests (d = 0.79) and outperformed learners in control groups (d = 0.57). The authors tested the effects of several moderators and found five to yield significant effects: effect sizes increased with publication year, were larger in EFL settings, for adults, when web instead of paper texts were used, and when ER was part of a course or offered as an extracurricular activity. In all cases, however, Jeon and Day warned that effects should be interpreted with caution, since particular studies (more recent studies, studies in EFL contexts, with adult learners, and studies where paper texts were used and where ER was part of a reading course) were heavily overrepresented. Finally, a meta-analysis by Liu and Zhang (2018) of 21 studies demonstrated an impact of extensive reading on foreign language learners' vocabulary learning; learners in ER programs scored better on posttests compared to pretests (d = 3.26 based on k = 21) and outperformed learners in control groups (d = 1.32 based on k = 17).

Title: THE IMPACT OF EXTENSIVE READING ON EFL UNIVERSITY STUDENTS’ ENGLISH LANGUAGE PROFICIENCY
Snippet: Extensive reading has been proven effective for the
development of EFL reading fluency. While previous studies
have investigated the impacts of ER on reading speed,
reading comprehension, and vocabulary knowledge, little
research has examined its effects on English language skills.
This research aimed to determine whether extensive reading
enhances the English language proficiency of EFL university
students. During the experiment, both the treatment and
control groups had 15 100-minute reading sessions, each
consisting of 50 minutes of intensive reading. In the second
part of the session, the treatment group could freely choose
books to read, while the control group continued intensive
reading activities. A pre-test and a post-test were used to
assess the participants’ language proficiency. The results
indicate that the treatment group outperformed the control
group. Based on the findings, several implications have been
suggested for English language practitioners, especially those
seeking methods to help their EFL students develop English
language proficiency.
Keywords: Extensive reading; English language proficiency;
reading fluency development; EFL reading.

Title: The influence of student engagement on the effects of an inferential reading comprehension intervention for struggling middle school readers
Snippet: Although many students benefit from evidence-based reading comprehension interventions, not all students will exhibit adequate response. Moderation analysis provides a statistical approach to examine for whom and under what conditions interventions are most effective. Conducted within a parent project, which investigated the effects of an inferential reading comprehension intervention, the current study examined factors related to the deployment of students’ attention as well as language status that might be associated with differential response to intervention. Sixty-six struggling middle school readers were randomly assigned to a computerized version of the intervention, a teacher-led version, or business-as-usual (BaU) control instruction. The influence of language status (i.e., English Learner status) and pre-intervention levels of mind-wandering, anxiety, and mindset on the effects of the inferential reading comprehension intervention were examined. There were no moderator effects for the teacher-led group compared to the BaU control. Conversely, anxiety, mind-wandering, and language status moderated the effects of the computer-led intervention for some reading and inference-making outcomes. The computer-led intervention was associated with improved inference-making for students with higher levels of self-reported anxiety and mind-wandering. In contrast, the computer-led intervention was less beneficial than BaU instruction for English learners. Findings are discussed with respect to how these factors might be relevant for interpreting the effects of interventions for struggling middle school readers in general, and for English learners in particular. The findings also point to the importance of considering the characteristics of both student and instructional features in the creation and testing of reading comprehension interventions.

Title: Fostering Cultural Understanding Through Vocabulary: The Case of Graded Readers
Snippet: Research exploring vocabulary learning has found that the input the learner receives and the number of word repetitions of this input are essential for vocabulary acquisition (Baddeley, 1990;Nation, 2001). In this regard, vocabulary acquisition and reading comprehension skills are closely related; vocabulary knowledge can improve reading comprehension skills. In turn, reading can contribute to vocabulary growth (Nation, 2001, Waring & Takaki, 2003). In EFL contexts, reading skills can be targeted by working on intensive or extensive reading. The former will refer to short texts (no more than 300-500 words) that allow teachers to focus on vocabulary and grammar structures. Extensive reading requires longer texts which, depending on their characteristics, can be aimed at either vocabulary growth or fluency development (Nation, 2001). For the purpose of this study, we will focus on the features of a text for vocabulary growth. Nation (2001) remarks that extensive reading should contain no more than 5% of unknown tokens and no less than 1%-2% to make sure that there is vocabulary to learn. In other words, so that learning can take place, the text cannot be too difficult to impede guessing from context. Moreover, texts that facilitate repetition of unknown vocabulary would provide favourable conditions for vocabulary learning (Waring & Takaki, 2003). The importance of spaced repetition and its effects in long term memory have already been stressed (Nation, 2001). However, it is not an easy task to establish the exact number of repetitions that are needed for a word to be learnt and other factors are also involved in this process. In the broadest sense, the rate of occurrences seems not to be less than six encounters and up to sixteen (Schmitt, 2000;Webb, 2007;Pellicer-Sánchez & Schmitt, 2010;Nation, 2014). Recent studies have reported that learners need to encounter new words at least 10 times in richly informative contexts to acquire them (Teng, 2016). 

Graded readers may serve the purpose of addressing both: fluency and vocabulary growth (Nation, 2001;McQuillan, 2016). In general, graded readers are adapted books for second language learners, characterized by their simple syntax and grammar, repetition of words and phrases, and use of vocabulary lists (Nation & Wang Ming-tzu, 1999).
</snippet>

Title: The Benefits of Graded Reading
Snippet: Doing large amounts of extensive reading at suitable levels of understanding is a productive tool to increase reading rate, vocabulary, motivation, attitude and general language proficiency. The amount of vocabulary and grammar learners has determines their language proficiency. Extensive reading enables learners to attain competencies in language skills. Graded readers are essential materials for doing extensive reading. They are particularly designed to enable learners practice reading skills and provide an opportunity to reinforce known vocabulary. Through multiple exposures learners become familiar with grammatical structures and vocabulary. Moreover, learners experience how they function in texts and they are motivated to use the vocabulary and structures they have learnt in their communication. Graded readers motivate learners, help them gain reading fluency, enhance their vocabulary and grammar knowledge development. This article defines extensive reading, emphasizes its contributions to language proficiency development and finally stresses out the role of grader readers in language learning.
</snippet>

Title: Unraveling the Affordances of 'Silas Marner' in a Japanese University EFL Context
Snippet: To facilitate easy, fluent reading-which, importantly, is presumed to optimize reading pleasure-the vocabulary in a graded reader is designed to be ninety-eight percent comprehensible (viz. level-appropriate) to the target learners, which, irrespective of level, normally amounts to two unknown words per page (Bamford & Day, 2004;Nation, 2014). Such simplifications or 'gradings' are based upon accountings of 'high frequency vocabulary,' identified according to standard word lists. The canonical General Service List of Words (West, 1950) and more recent Academic Word List (Coxhead, 2000) have been commonly employed. Software-enabled corpus analysis, now routinely performed with ease, greatly facilitates the grading of authentic texts. If a text features vocabulary items identified as overly rare, or if the proportion of lower-frequency items is too high, then the inappropriate items are duly replaced, comporting with prescribed standards of 'difficulty' for the desired level or 'grade.' 

Other research refutes the purported effectiveness of graded readers, however. The work of Waring and Takaki (2003), for instance, points to the lack of convincing evidence that regular graded reading positively affects incidental vocabulary acquisition. Horst (2005) shows that significant incidental vocabulary acquisition requires learners to read impractically large quantities of graded material. Moreover, Cobb (2007) contends that graded reading alone provides insufficient input to foster comprehension of complex texts. The apparent problem is that, even after an active, comprehensive course of graded reading, learners are simply not exposed to enough unknown or unfamiliar language (Grabe & Stoller, 2002). Nation (2014), a leading researcher of L2 vocabulary acquisition and proponent of graded reading, claims that, to read unsimplified texts, a learner must have amassed an English vocabulary that includes the 9000 most frequently used words. Nation acknowledges, too, that only the first 3000 words are normally included in even the highest-level graded readers. If these are designed at each level to feature only two expectedly unknown words per page, then graded reading seems inapt preparation for tackling complex texts, in which many more lower frequency terms expectedly appear. Simply put, stepping stones serve little purpose if they terminate midstream.
</snippet>

Title: Assessing Reading Strategies of Engineering Students: Think Aloud Approach
Snippet: Findings of the verbal reports of the successful readers indicate that these readers related their personal experience and empathized with the information presented in the text. By relating their observations of the real world with the text, successful readers could grasp the meaning. While processing the information, a successful reader was found to be using simplification strategies like processing the meaning of words by using synonyms. 

The partly successful readers made limited use of cognitive skills whereas the unsuccessful readers even less. 

The verbal reports of the partly successful engineering students and unsuccessful students reveal that they read the words in isolation and do not make an attempt to understand the meaning of the complete sentence. These students try to grasp every word and thus end up spending too much time on a word without understanding its meaning. However, good readers made connections with their own experiences and related the new information to their prior knowledge. Unsuccessful and some of the partly successful readers were found ignoring punctuation and thus found the phrases and sentences as meaningless combination of words. While processing the information from academic related texts, successful readers were able to identify the devices which were used to appeal and influence their thinking. The verbal reports of successful readers indicate that they read extensively. Extensive reading broadens and increases vocabulary knowledge and this is important for effective communication and comprehension. Habit of reading extensively also gave them confidence while regular reading habits enhanced their concentration skills by expanding their attention span. Partly successful readers could understand parts of the text. However, English teachers need to give more training in the use of reading strategies to make these readers to move a step ahead in understanding the meaning and reach them to the level of successful readers. The problems of unsuccessful readers are enormous. Most of these readers lack proficiency in English language skills. Lack of basic knowledge in sentence structures and the usage of vocabulary in different contexts is an obstacle for the reading proficiency. Through extensive reading tasks, English teachers have to give language input and also train these students in the use of reading strategies. During the intensive reading activities, these unsuccessful readers have to be given individual attention in cognitive skills.

Title: The Effect of Graded Readers on Reading Comprehension Skill of EFL Students
Snippet: For language teachers, how to promote proficient reading is an important issue. In the ESL and EFL context, there is a tendency towards the use of skill-building textbooks and procedures. Little attention has been given to extensive reading for pleasure as a means to improve comprehension, and the value of extensive reading is overlooked most of the time though many extensive reading studies have shown that extensive reading has a long-term effect on language learners' reading development and also on overall language proficiency. What needs to be done is to incorporate extensive reading into the curriculum. The present study therefore provides further evidence regarding how reading extensively via graded readers contributes to reading development of language learners . 

The results of the present study also indicated that the reading program based on graded readers, to which the extensive reading group were exposed, brought about much more satisfying gains in reading comprehension than the traditional close reading techniques applied to the control group. Significant difference on gains in reading comprehension strongly suggests that an extensive reading program based on graded readers is much more beneficial to the development of reading comprehension than traditional reading lessons based on the close study of short texts. 

On the other hand, the other research question of the current study was to reveal if the number of books read by the students took part in the experimental group had effect on the reading comprehension development of the students. For this reason, students in the experimental group were divided into two sub-groups, and the numbers of books read by the students who participated in the extensive reading program were compared. This comparison showed that students who read more books scored significantly better than the other students reading less books. Thus, we got a favorable result for the effect of the amount of reading on the reading comprehension development of the students. 

We may conclude, therefore, that reading comprehension will develop naturally if learners are motivated to read interesting simplified materials like graded readers. The extensive reading program based on graded readers has led to much greater improvement in learners' reading comprehension than traditional language activities. Although one of the stated objectives of the material used by subjects in the control group was a 'close and detailed understanding of the text', it appears that this approach is much less successful in developing comprehension than providing learners with attractive, high-interest story books, which learners are well-motivated to read and understand.
</snippet>

Title: The Effects of Control for Ability Level on EFL Reading of Graded
Snippet: AbstractThe study was aimed to examine how EFL learners of English reacted to graded readers in terms of reading strategy use, comprehension, speed, and attitude as well as motivation when control for ability level was determined. When moving through other graded readers at the same level the numbers of strategies utilized by males and females were different at the 0.05 level of significance and the time spent on reading decreased on average. Title: Extended Reading: A Teacher-Directed Alternative to Extensive Reading
Snippet: Extensive reading is an approach that gives maximum freedom to students to read independently and as much as possible. In a traditional extensive reading approach, students read at least a graded reader every week in order to maximize reading practice. Students select their own texts, usually at a level slightly below their linguistic level. They are encouraged to read rapidly without using dictionaries. They read for pleasure and comprehension, and traditionally are not tested on what they have read. The teacher's role is to monitor their reading, keep track of their reading habits, and manage the program. Goals of such a program include developing positive attitude, confidence, and motivation, increasing reading speed and fluency, increasing word recognition ability, and understanding purpose in reading (Day & Bamford, 1998). 

Simplified texts may be preferable to authentic texts. If authentic texts are too difficult, students will go back to old habits of focusing on deciphering the code, using dictionaries, not reading fluently, and developing negative feelings about reading. The level of i minus 1, just under their linguistic ability, is defined as students' comfort zone, and students should start out reading at this level, though over the course of an extensive reading program they should ladder up and read more difficult graded texts (Day & Bamford, 1998). Students should also read texts that interest them, and abandon them if their interest falls. They should not try to push ahead with difficult or uninteresting texts, as this may reduce the pleasure of reading (Day & Bamford 1998). 

Successful results have been widely reported with extensive reading programs, with most research being carried out in Asia. Significant gains were made on TOEFL scores after a two-month extensive reading program in Singapore, and the use of extensive reading was a better indicator of reading progress than the amount of previous English study (Renandya, Rejan, & Jacobs, 1999). In Japan, low level readers who participated in extensive reading programs nearly caught up with high level readers in traditional intensive reading programs. This was shown to be true in both more prestigious and less prestigious institutions (Mason & Krashen, 1997).
</snippet>

Title: Extended Reading: A Teacher-Directed Alternative to Extensive Reading
Snippet: Extensive reading programs have been shown to improve reading proficiency faster than traditional intensive reading programs alone (Nakanishi, 2015). Extensive reading programs are sometimes done instead of intensive reading courses, with reading done in class in an informal atmosphere, or alternatively, in addition to an intensive reading program, as a self-moderated out-of-class activity. 

While the study described in this paper was done in the United States, it is directly relevant to Asian students and teachers, and to Asian teaching contexts, in two ways. First, extensive reading is very commonly used in Asia, and is perhaps nowhere more widespread than in Japan (Mason & Krashen, 1997;Reed & Goldberg, 2008;Stoekel, Reagan, & Hann, 2012;Nakanishi 2015). Second, the study was conducted with primarily Asian students so likely the results can be directly applied to Asian learning environments. 

Sustaining an extensive reading program requires highly self-motivated students. If students entering IEPs are less motivated to study independently, it is doubtful whether they would follow through with an extensive reading program where outcomes are not directly assessed. The length of texts in an extensive reading program may also serve to frustrate many unmotivated students, so rather than fostering enjoyment of reading, such a program may only serve to discourage them more. 

This report will review a technique, developed at an IEP in a large public university in the United States, which seeks to bridge the gap between intensive and extensive reading, and make independent reading of longer texts accessible to less motivated students at the intermediate level. This technique, called extended reading, also presents authentic texts to students who may otherwise limit their reading to textbook passages. Rather than asking students to read entire books (usually graded readers) which are below their level, extended reading requires students to independently read much shorter selections (4 to 10 pages weekly), and take short quizzes that test comprehension of main ideas. Results of a small-scale experimental-control design research project indicate that gains in reading proficiency are made by students using the extended reading method over those whose reading is restricted to classroom managed intensive reading.
</snippet>

Summary of average effects and moderators

1) Comprehensible input, vocabulary coverage, and exposure frequency
- ER works when texts are sufficiently comprehensible and provide repeated, spaced encounters with new words in rich contexts; this boosts vocabulary growth, which in turn raises comprehension and fluency. <cite id="f5ea37ef-0">Vocabulary acquisition depends on input and repeated encounters; texts for vocabulary growth should have ≤5% unknown tokens (with ≥1–2% target), enabling learners to guess from context and accumulate long-term retention via spaced repetition on the order of 6–16 encounters, with recent work suggesting ≥10 high-quality encounters</cite> <cite id="f5ea37ef-2">Reviews converge on lexical coverage, incidental vs. direct vocabulary learning, rate of new word learning from graded readers, and the role of instructional support for lexis in driving reading comprehension</cite>.
- Graded readers can optimize coverage and motivation; however, their simplicity can also limit exposure to lower-frequency academic vocabulary, making unsupervised graded reading alone insufficient for complex text comprehension without scaffolding. <cite id="f5ea37ef-1">Graded readers increase vocabulary, fluency, and motivation through multiple exposures and reinforcement of known lexicon</cite> <cite id="f5ea37ef-3">Graded readers often target ~98% comprehensible input (≈2 unknowns/page), but critics argue they expose learners to too few lower-frequency terms, requiring impractically large quantities for incidental gains and insufficient input for complex texts without additional instruction</cite>.
- Responsiveness varies by how well a student’s reading level and interests align to text difficulty and dose. Students who read more books in ER programs show larger comprehension gains, indicating a dose-response pattern that depends on sustained motivation and access. <cite id="10663c84-0">Students who read more books in an ER program scored significantly higher on reading comprehension than peers who read fewer books, supporting a dose–response</cite> <cite id="10663c84-2">ER emphasizes i–1 to i-level texts for comfort and fluency, with learners abandoning uninteresting or too-difficult materials; motivation and interest are central to maintaining sufficient dose</cite>.

2) Strategy repertoire, metacognition, and prior content knowledge
- ER often co-trains strategies (e.g., inference, simplification, connecting to prior knowledge), which mediate comprehension and transfer to independent reading. Students who actively use strategies and connect text to experience show higher comprehension and fluency; those with weaker strategy use lag behind. <cite id="10663c84-4">Participants’ reading logs showed wide text variety, with prior or content knowledge aiding later comprehension; prior knowledge significantly contributes to reading comprehension and can offset linguistic deficiencies</cite> <cite id="f5ea37ef-4">Successful readers relate real-world experiences and use simplification strategies and connections to prior knowledge; unsuccessful readers get bogged down by word-by-word decoding and lack of contextual knowledge</cite>.
- Baseline cognitive and executive resources shape how ER texts are processed. Learners with stronger executive function (EF) show better reading performance across L1 and L2; SES-related advantages in EF can indirectly amplify ER gains by improving comprehension and text integration. <cite id="1ab583e4-3">Executive function uniquely predicts L1 and L2 reading comprehension and mediates SES effects; SES directly predicts L2 reading comprehension and its indirect path increases with EF, with EF effects remaining after age control</cite>.
- Affective states and mind-wandering modulate learning during reading-intensive interventions; these effects generalize to ER-like settings. Students with higher anxiety or mind-wandering can benefit from structured, paced digital ER (suggesting scaffolding helps regulate off-task thoughts), whereas English learners may respond less well to certain ER formats than monolingual peers, highlighting cultural/language-status contingencies. <cite id="1ab583e4-4">Anxiety, mind-wandering, and language status moderated benefits of a computerized inferential reading intervention; a teacher-led version showed no moderation, underscoring how student and instructional features shape differential response</cite>.

3) Output- and accountability-driven consolidation
- When ER is coupled with low-stakes output (e.g., reading logs, summaries, dictogloss), accountability cues increase attention and memory consolidation. <cite id="10663c84-0">ER programs that incorporated graded readers outperformed traditional close-reading instruction, with larger gains accompanying higher book counts</cite> <cite id="10663c84-3">An extended reading approach with short quizzes improved reading proficiency over classroom-only intensive reading, suggesting that manageable text length plus comprehension checks supported less-motivated intermediate learners</cite>.
- Writing and spelling often improve via ER due to repeated exposure to cohesive structures and discourse patterns, which learners can reimagine in short outputs; responsiveness varies with initial writing proficiency and willingness to produce. <cite id="10663c84-1">Writing and spelling gains have been reported alongside ER use, with learners increasing strategy use, speed, comprehension, attitude, and motivation when texts are matched to ability</cite>.

Who benefits more—and why—and when benefits are smaller or null

- Older, more instructed learners and in EFL contexts: ER effects tend to be larger for adults and in EFL settings, possibly due to greater autonomy, clearer curricular alignment, and sustained, course-integrated accountability. <cite id="1ab583e4-1">Effects were larger for adults and in EFL settings, with course-integrated ER outperforming extracurricular or poorly supported variants after publication-year adjustments</cite>.
- High-dose, well-matched texts with support: Students who complete more books, have access to leveled libraries, and receive guidance on selection and monitoring show larger gains; unmotivated or unsupported learners plateau or regress. <cite id="10663c84-0">More books read correlated with higher comprehension</cite> <cite id="10663c84-2">Students should read texts of i–1/i-level of interest; traditional ER without assessment can discourage unmotivated learners</cite> <cite id="10663c84-3">Without structure, less-motivated learners may avoid longer texts; extended reading with short quizzes improved outcomes over intensive-only classes</cite>.
- Strong EF and prior knowledge: Learners with higher EF and stronger background knowledge benefit more because they integrate new lexical items into schema and sustain on-task behavior; SES-linked EF advantages can widen ER-driven proficiency gaps unless programs explicitly scaffold schema and metacognition. <cite id="1ab583e4-3">EF uniquely predicts reading abilities and mediates SES effects on L2 reading; SES directly predicts L2 reading comprehension</cite> <cite id="10663c84-4">Prior knowledge enhances comprehension and can compensate for linguistic deficiencies</cite>.
- Motivation, autonomy, and affect: Intrinsically motivated students, especially those with high interest in chosen texts, show larger gains; anxiety and mind-wandering reduce benefits unless addressed by structured scaffolds. <cite id="10663c84-2">Choice at comfortable difficulty is recommended to sustain pleasure and fluency; abandoning uninteresting texts prevents demotivation</cite> <cite id="1ab583e4-4">Anxiety and mind-wandering moderated ER-like intervention outcomes; structured formats helped, while English learner status reduced benefit in one condition</cite>.
- Program fit and materials: Overly simplified graded readers can limit academic vocabulary exposure without additional support; authentic but too-difficult texts induce decoding focus and demotivation. Students for whom English background knowledge and academic lexicon are weak may need explicit vocabulary and discourse scaffolds to realize ER gains. <cite id="f5ea37ef-3">Graded reading alone may underexpose learners to lower-frequency academic vocabulary; unsupervised reading may be insufficient for complex texts</cite> <cite id="10663c84-2">Authentic texts that are too difficult push students back into decoding and dictionary reliance; gradual “laddering” up difficulty and following interest mitigate this</cite>.

Failure modes and equity considerations
- Misaligned difficulty and low interest reduce fluency practice and demotivate learners, blunting gains; without accountability, dose falls and benefits diminish. <cite id="10663c84-2">Reading below level for pleasure without monitoring can collapse into inefficient decoding; ER aims to keep students in their comfort zone and follow interest to avoid discouragement</cite> <cite id="10663c84-3">Unmotivated students often disengage from long texts without assessment or manageable chunks</cite>.
- Overreliance on graded readers without scaffolding for academic vocabulary and inference can leave lower-SES or lower-proficiency learners with ceiling effects, as exposure to high-frequency lists alone may not build the lexicon and discourse competence needed for complex texts. <cite id="f5ea37ef-3">Graded readers may not supply enough lower-frequency vocabulary for complex texts without additional instruction</cite>.
- Language-status and affective contingencies can accentuate disparities. English learners may gain less from certain technology-mediated ER formats than peers in supportive, teacher-led models; anxiety and mind-wandering further depress responsiveness, indicating a need for targeted supports. <cite id="1ab583e4-4">English learners benefited less from a computer-led intervention; anxiety and mind-wandering moderated gains, whereas teacher-led instruction showed no moderation</cite>.
- Measured heterogeneity sometimes reflects sampling and methodological imbalances; recent-year, EFL, adult, and web-based ER studies dominate literature, complicating simple subgroup comparisons. <cite id="1ab583e4-1">Moderator patterns (e.g., larger effects in EFL, adults, web texts, course-integrated programs) may reflect overrepresentation of specific study types and publication-year inflation, warranting caution in subgroup claims</cite>.

Practical levers to reduce heterogeneity and widen high-end gains
- Calibrate difficulty and dose: Use leveled books with 95/1–2% unknown-token guidelines; ensure ≥10 high-quality encounters for new words; track and adjust reading logs to maintain interest and manageable length. <cite id="f5ea37ef-0">Target ≤5% unknown tokens with ≥1–2% intentional new vocabulary, and provide repeated, spaced encounters for durable learning</cite> <cite id="f5ea37ef-3">Design for ~98% comprehensible input (~2 unknowns/page) while supplementing lower-frequency vocabulary</cite>.
- Add scaffolds that convert input to output: brief daily summaries, dictogloss, reading journals tied to formative feedback, and periodic quizzes to create accountability without undermining pleasure. <cite id="10663c84-3">Short weekly quizzes improved proficiency beyond intensive-only classes and supported less-motivated students</cite> <cite id="10663c84-0">Accountability and dose (more books read) correlated with higher comprehension</cite>.
- Build schema and strategy explicitly: teach inference, activation of prior knowledge, and simplification strategies; integrate content-focused pre-reading to connect new texts to learners’ experiences. <cite id="10663c84-4">Connecting real-world knowledge and using simplification/inference strategies is characteristic of successful readers; instruction in strategies can move partly/unsusccessful readers toward proficiency</cite>.
- Address EF and affect: embed brief self-regulation routines (planning–monitoring–reflecting), provide structured pacing, and offer choices to regulate mind-wandering and anxiety; for English learners, add bilingual support and culturally responsive texts. <cite id="1ab583e4-4">Structured formats helped students with higher anxiety and mind-wandering; EL status reduced benefits in one condition, underscoring the need for tailored supports</cite> <cite id="1ab583e4-3">EF uniquely predicts reading success; SES advantages via EF can indirectly shape ER responsiveness</cite>.
- Align to curriculum and assessment: integrate ER with writing tasks and speaking presentations; time ER during class and include low-stakes accountability to ensure exposure translates into curricular outcomes. <cite id="1ab583e4-1">ER integrated into courses shows larger effects than purely extracurricular, ungraded versions</cite> <cite id="10663c84-1">ER improves writing and comprehension when texts are matched to ability and sustained</cite>.

Putting it together: a mechanistic map of heterogeneity
- ER improves proficiency by increasing lexical coverage and repetition (vocabulary), building fluency and comprehension through comfortable, high-interest dose, and expanding background knowledge that supports inference; these gains are mediated by strategy use and EF resources, and amplified by structured accountability and output tasks. <cite id="f5ea37ef-0">Vocabulary growth depends on sufficient, repeated, and spaced encounters with comprehensible input</cite> <cite id="10663c84-4">Prior knowledge and strategy use enhance comprehension and can compensate for linguistic deficiencies</cite> <cite id="10663c84-3">Accountability via short quizzes improved outcomes over intensive-only classes</cite>.
- Responsiveness varies because learners differ in baseline vocabulary, EF, motivation, strategy knowledge, and prior content domains; instructional fit (difficulty, interest, autonomy supports, scaffolds) determines whether input converts into durable gains. <cite id="1ab583e4-0">Learner, intervention, and study-level moderators systematically shape ER outcomes</cite> <cite id="1ab583e4-1">Adults, EFL contexts, web texts, and course-integrated ER show larger effects on average, with cautions on sampling</cite> <cite id="f5ea37ef-3">Graded readers can underexpose learners to academic vocabulary without additional scaffolding</cite>.
- Programs that optimize comprehensible input, strategy scaffolding, accountable output, and culturally responsive materials will narrow the ER response gap by supporting the mechanisms that underlie large gains for high-SES, motivated, and higher-proficiency students, while also unlocking growth among lower-SES and lower-proficiency learners who need explicit supports to overcome EF, vocabulary, and affective barriers. <cite id="1ab583e4-3">SES advantages operate partly via EF; targeted EF and schema supports can make ER benefits more equitable</cite> <cite id="10663c84-4">Reading logs and content-knowledge activation can raise comprehension and close gaps</cite>.

Limitations and next steps
- Some reported moderator effects reflect publication and sampling biases; triangulation across classroom, web-based, and long-term implementations is needed to isolate true heterogeneity mechanisms. <cite id="1ab583e4-1">Effect sizes may be inflated and subgroups overrepresented; caution is warranted in subgroup interpretations</cite>.
- Direct mediation tests linking specific ER features to vocabulary growth, strategy gains, and proficiency over time remain scarce; randomized studies that measure encounters, dictionary use, strategy use, and EF/affect trajectories alongside proficiency would sharpen causal inferences. <cite id="1ab583e4-0">Meta-analytic moderators identify candidate mechanisms, but causal mediation within ER programs is under-tested</cite>.

In sum, ER’s uneven effects arise from differential access to effective comprehensible input, variability in learners’ cognitive-affective resources and strategy repertoires, and differences in program fit and accountability. Closing the gap requires calibrating difficulty and dose to interest, adding structured output and strategy scaffolds, and explicitly supporting EF and background knowledge—especially for learners who face vocabulary, motivation, and affective barriers without tailored interventions. <cite id="f5ea37ef-0">Vocabulary coverage, repetition, and spaced exposure</cite> <cite id="10663c84-0">Dose-response with more books read</cite> <cite id="10663c84-2">Comfort-zone text selection and interest</cite> <cite id="1ab583e4-1">Course-integrated and well-supported ER</cite> <cite id="1ab583e4-3">EF and SES pathways to reading success</cite> <cite id="1ab583e4-4">Affective and language-status contingencies</cite>.
</answer>

Title: Learning a Language Through Reading: A Meta-analysis of Studies on the Effects of Extensive Reading on Second and Foreign Language Learning
Snippet: In this meta-analysis, we aimed to gain more insight into the characteristics of extensive reading that contribute to its success. Our study was built up around two research questions: 

1. What are the effects of extensive reading on the development of learners' second and foreign language skills? 

This question allowed us to update the conclusions of previous meta-analyses. We defined both "learners" and "language skills" broadly: we targeted child, adolescent, and adult learners, and we included multiple language domains: decoding and fluency, grammar, reading comprehension, reading motivation, speaking, vocabulary, and writing. Sample moderators (a) are learner type (i.e., second vs. foreign language learners), first language of participants (same vs. different), and educational level (primary, secondary, tertiary education, other). Intervention moderators (b) are interventionist (was the intervention executed by a researcher?), whether or not the intervention included text limitation, help with text selection, accountability, help/ instruction before or during ER, interaction, rewards, a digital support program, home activities, the provision of books at home, graded readers, the type of text medium, and the duration of the intervention in weeks. Study moderators (c) are peer review, design (quasi-experimental vs. experimental), random assignment, randomization level, and study quality. We will discuss elaborate definitions of these moderators in the Method section.

Title: Learning a Language Through Reading: A Meta-analysis of Studies on the Effects of Extensive Reading on Second and Foreign Language Learning
Snippet: A meta-analysis by Nakanishi (2015) of 34 pretest-posttest comparisons, including 18 experimental vs. control group studies, showed that extensive reading is effective in promoting second language learners' reading proficiency, including reading speed, reading comprehension, vocabulary, and grammar; learners in ER programs scored better on posttests compared to pretests (d = 0.71) and outperformed learners in control groups (d = 0.46). Nakanishi additionally tested whether intervention effects were affected by learners' age and length of instruction. His conclusions were ambivalent: he suggested that "the effect of extensive reading increases with older participants" (p. 26) and that "longer length of instruction period could improve students' proficiency in English" (p. 27), but at the same time had to conclude there were no statistically significant differences among subgroups. A meta-analysis by Jeon and Day (2016) of 51 experimental vs. control group studies and 20 pre-post design studies revealed a positive effect of extensive reading on learners' reading proficiency, including reading rate, reading comprehension, and vocabulary; learners in ER programs scored better on posttests than pretests (d = 0.79) and outperformed learners in control groups (d = 0.57). The authors tested the effects of several moderators and found five to yield significant effects: effect sizes increased with publication year, were larger in EFL settings, for adults, when web instead of paper texts were used, and when ER was part of a course or offered as an extracurricular activity. In all cases, however, Jeon and Day warned that effects should be interpreted with caution, since particular studies (more recent studies, studies in EFL contexts, with adult learners, and studies where paper texts were used and where ER was part of a reading course) were heavily overrepresented. Finally, a meta-analysis by Liu and Zhang (2018) of 21 studies demonstrated an impact of extensive reading on foreign language learners' vocabulary learning; learners in ER programs scored better on posttests compared to pretests (d = 3.26 based on k = 21) and outperformed learners in control groups (d = 1.32 based on k = 17).

Title: THE IMPACT OF EXTENSIVE READING ON EFL UNIVERSITY STUDENTS’ ENGLISH LANGUAGE PROFICIENCY
Snippet: Extensive reading has been proven effective for the
development of EFL reading fluency. While previous studies
have investigated the impacts of ER on reading speed,
reading comprehension, and vocabulary knowledge, little
research has examined its effects on English language skills.
This research aimed to determine whether extensive reading
enhances the English language proficiency of EFL university
students. During the experiment, both the treatment and
control groups had 15 100-minute reading sessions, each
consisting of 50 minutes of intensive reading. In the second
part of the session, the treatment group could freely choose
books to read, while the control group continued intensive
reading activities. A pre-test and a post-test were used to
assess the participants’ language proficiency. The results
indicate that the treatment group outperformed the control
group. Based on the findings, several implications have been
suggested for English language practitioners, especially those
seeking methods to help their EFL students develop English
language proficiency.
Keywords: Extensive reading; English language proficiency;
reading fluency development; EFL reading.

Title: Socioeconomic Account of Reading Abilities in Learning Chinese as a First Language and English as a Second Language
Snippet: The present study demonstrated the importance of SES and EF in L1 Chinese and L2 English reading abilities for Hong Kong Chinese-English bilingual students at the ages of 8-11 years. In particular, the SEM showed the unique role of EF in both L1 Chinese and L2 English reading abilities and its mediation in the relationship between SES and reading abilities when age was controlled  Note. SES = socioeconomic status; EF = executive function; L1 = first language; L2 = second language. Age was controlled in the analysis. 

for. SES directly predicted L2 English reading comprehension in addition to its indirect contribution to L2 English reading comprehension via EF. Although individual differences in language proficiency were not specifically examined as a moderator, it is important to note that the four levels of reading outcomes do vary in their levels of difficulty. The findings suggest that EF exerts significant mediation effects across all four reading tasks, which vary in terms of language proficiency (L1/L2) and difficulty levels (in terms of words, short, and long passages). On the other hand, SES seems to become less influential as language proficiency advances, especially considering that the current participants exhibit greater proficiency in their L1 compared to their L2.

Title: The influence of student engagement on the effects of an inferential reading comprehension intervention for struggling middle school readers
Snippet: Although many students benefit from evidence-based reading comprehension interventions, not all students will exhibit adequate response. Moderation analysis provides a statistical approach to examine for whom and under what conditions interventions are most effective. Conducted within a parent project, which investigated the effects of an inferential reading comprehension intervention, the current study examined factors related to the deployment of students’ attention as well as language status that might be associated with differential response to intervention. Sixty-six struggling middle school readers were randomly assigned to a computerized version of the intervention, a teacher-led version, or business-as-usual (BaU) control instruction. The influence of language status (i.e., English Learner status) and pre-intervention levels of mind-wandering, anxiety, and mindset on the effects of the inferential reading comprehension intervention were examined. There were no moderator effects for the teacher-led group compared to the BaU control. Conversely, anxiety, mind-wandering, and language status moderated the effects of the computer-led intervention for some reading and inference-making outcomes. The computer-led intervention was associated with improved inference-making for students with higher levels of self-reported anxiety and mind-wandering. In contrast, the computer-led intervention was less beneficial than BaU instruction for English learners. Findings are discussed with respect to how these factors might be relevant for interpreting the effects of interventions for struggling middle school readers in general, and for English learners in particular. The findings also point to the importance of considering the characteristics of both student and instructional features in the creation and testing of reading comprehension interventions.

documents.snippet: A meta-analysis by Nakanishi (2015) of 34 pretest-posttest comparisons, including 18 experimental vs. control group studies, showed that extensive reading is effective in promoting second language learners' reading proficiency, including reading speed, reading comprehension, vocabulary, and grammar; learners in ER programs scored better on posttests compared to pretests (d = 0.71) and outperformed learners in control groups (d = 0.46). Nakanishi additionally tested whether intervention effects were affected by learners' age and length of instruction. His conclusions were ambivalent: he suggested that "the effect of extensive reading increases with older participants" (p. 26) and that "longer length of instruction period could improve students' proficiency in English" (p. 27), but at the same time had to conclude there were no statistically significant differences among subgroups. A meta-analysis by Jeon and Day (2016) of 51 experimental vs. control group studies and 20 pre-post design studies revealed a positive effect of extensive reading on learners' reading proficiency, including reading rate, reading comprehension, and vocabulary; learners in ER programs scored better on posttests than pretests (d = 0.79) and outperformed learners in control groups (d = 0.57). The authors tested the effects of several moderators and found five to yield significant effects: effect sizes increased with publication year, were larger in EFL settings, for adults, when web instead of paper texts were used, and when ER was part of a course or offered as an extracurricular activity. In all cases, however, Jeon and Day warned that effects should be interpreted with caution, since particular studies (more recent studies, studies in EFL contexts, with adult learners, and studies where paper texts were used and where ER was part of a reading course) were heavily overrepresented. Finally, a meta-analysis by Liu and Zhang (2018) of 21 studies demonstrated an impact of extensive reading on foreign language learners' vocabulary learning; learners in ER programs scored better on posttests compared to pretests (d = 3.26 based on k = 21) and outperformed learners in control groups (d = 1.32 based on k = 17).

documents.title: THE IMPACT OF EXTENSIVE READING ON EFL UNIVERSITY STUDENTS’ ENGLISH LANGUAGE PROFICIENCY
documents.snippet:
Extensive reading has been proven effective for the
development of EFL reading fluency. While previous studies
have investigated the impacts of ER on reading speed,
reading comprehension, and vocabulary knowledge, little
research has examined its effects on English language skills.
This research aimed to determine whether extensive reading
enhances the English language proficiency of EFL university
students. During the experiment, both the treatment and
control groups had 15 100-minute reading sessions, each
consisting of 50 minutes of intensive reading. In the second
part of the session, the treatment group could freely choose
books to read, while the control group continued intensive
reading activities. A pre-test and a post-test were used to
assess the participants’ language proficiency. The results
indicate that the treatment group outperformed the control
group. Based on the findings, several implications have been
suggested for English language practitioners, especially those
seeking methods to help their EFL students develop English
language proficiency.
Keywords: Extensive reading; English language proficiency;
reading fluency development; EFL reading.

documents.title: Socioeconomic Account of Reading Abilities in Learning Chinese as a First Language and English as a Second Language
documents.snippet:
The present study demonstrated the importance of SES and EF in L1 Chinese and L2 English reading abilities for Hong Kong Chinese-English bilingual students at the ages of 8-11 years. In particular, the SEM showed the unique role of EF in both L1 Chinese and L2 English reading abilities and its mediation in the relationship between SES and reading abilities when age was controlled  Note. SES = socioeconomic status; EF = executive function; L1 = first language; L2 = second language. Age was controlled in the analysis. 

for. SES directly predicted L2 English reading comprehension in addition to its indirect contribution to L2 English reading comprehension via EF. Although individual differences in language proficiency were not specifically examined as a moderator, it is important to note that the four levels of reading outcomes do vary in their levels of difficulty. The findings suggest that EF exerts significant mediation effects across all four reading tasks, which vary in terms of language proficiency (L1/L2) and difficulty levels (in terms of words, short, and long passages). On the other hand, SES seems to become less influential as language proficiency advances, especially considering that the current participants exhibit greater proficiency in their L1 compared to their L2.

documents.title: The influence of student engagement on the effects of an inferential reading comprehension intervention for struggling middle school readers
documents.snippet: Although many students benefit from evidence-based reading comprehension interventions, not all students will exhibit adequate response. Moderation analysis provides a statistical approach to examine for whom and under what conditions interventions are most effective. Conducted within a parent project, which investigated the effects of an inferential reading comprehension intervention, the current study examined factors related to the deployment of students’ attention as well as language status that might be associated with differential response to intervention. Sixty-six struggling middle school readers were randomly assigned to a computerized version of the intervention, a teacher-led version, or business-as-usual (BaU) control instruction. The influence of language status (i.e., English Learner status) and pre-intervention levels of mind-wandering, anxiety, and mindset on the effects of the inferential reading comprehension intervention were examined. There were no moderator effects for the teacher-led group compared to the BaU control. Conversely, anxiety, mind-wandering, and language status moderated the effects of the computer-led intervention for some reading and inference-making outcomes. The computer-led intervention was associated with improved inference-making for students with higher levels of self-reported anxiety and mind-wandering. In contrast, the computer-led intervention was less beneficial than BaU instruction for English learners. Findings are discussed with respect to how these factors might be relevant for interpreting the effects of interventions for struggling middle school readers in general, and for English learners in particular. The findings also point to the importance of considering the characteristics of both student and instructional features in the creation and testing of reading comprehension interventions.

Title: Fostering Cultural Understanding Through Vocabulary: The Case of Graded Readers
Snippet: Research exploring vocabulary learning has found that the input the learner receives and the number of word repetitions of this input are essential for vocabulary acquisition (Baddeley, 1990;Nation, 2001). In this regard, vocabulary acquisition and reading comprehension skills are closely related; vocabulary knowledge can improve reading comprehension skills. In turn, reading can contribute to vocabulary growth (Nation, 2001, Waring & Takaki, 2003). In EFL contexts, reading skills can be targeted by working on intensive or extensive reading. The former will refer to short texts (no more than 300-500 words) that allow teachers to focus on vocabulary and grammar structures. Extensive reading requires longer texts which, depending on their characteristics, can be aimed at either vocabulary growth or fluency development (Nation, 2001). For the purpose of this study, we will focus on the features of a text for vocabulary growth. Nation (2001) remarks that extensive reading should contain no more than 5% of unknown tokens and no less than 1%-2% to make sure that there is vocabulary to learn. In other words, so that learning can take place, the text cannot be too difficult to impede guessing from context. Moreover, texts that facilitate repetition of unknown vocabulary would provide favourable conditions for vocabulary learning (Waring & Takaki, 2003). The importance of spaced repetition and its effects in long term memory have already been stressed (Nation, 2001). However, it is not an easy task to establish the exact number of repetitions that are needed for a word to be learnt and other factors are also involved in this process. In the broadest sense, the rate of occurrences seems not to be less than six encounters and up to sixteen (Schmitt, 2000;Webb, 2007;Pellicer-Sánchez & Schmitt, 2010;Nation, 2014). Recent studies have reported that learners need to encounter new words at least 10 times in richly informative contexts to acquire them (Teng, 2016). 

Graded readers may serve the purpose of addressing both: fluency and vocabulary growth (Nation, 2001;McQuillan, 2016). In general, graded readers are adapted books for second language learners, characterized by their simple syntax and grammar, repetition of words and phrases, and use of vocabulary lists (Nation & Wang Ming-tzu, 1999).

Title: The Benefits of Graded Reading
Snippet: Doing large amounts of extensive reading at suitable levels of understanding is a productive tool to increase reading rate, vocabulary, motivation, attitude and general language proficiency. The amount of vocabulary and grammar learners has determines their language proficiency. Extensive reading enables learners to attain competencies in language skills. Graded readers are essential materials for doing extensive reading. They are particularly designed to enable learners practice reading skills and provide an opportunity to reinforce known vocabulary. Through multiple exposures learners become familiar with grammatical structures and vocabulary. Moreover, learners experience how they function in texts and they are motivated to use the vocabulary and structures they have learnt in their communication. Graded readers motivate learners, help them gain reading fluency, enhance their vocabulary and grammar knowledge development. This article defines extensive reading, emphasizes its contributions to language proficiency development and finally stresses out the role of grader readers in language learning.
